Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

Powder Bed Fusion in Polymers and Metals

Follow the shared powder-layer cycle, then distinguish polymer SLS and MJF from stated metal laser and electron-beam routes.

Powder bed fusion repeats a spread, select, and lower cycle

Powder bed fusion repeats a spread, select, and lower cycle

Powder bed fusion (PBF) is one additive-manufacturing family. A machine spreads a thin powder layer, applies thermal energy to selected regions, lowers or advances the build, and repeats. Unselected powder remains around the growing parts until they are unpacked.

The family name does not specify one material or energy source. Polymer and metal examples can share the layer cycle while differing in temperature, atmosphere, thermal behavior, support strategy, cooldown, powder recovery, postprocessing and inspection.

Start with Additive Manufacturing Process Families for the seven-family map. PBF thermally fuses powder during the build; it is not binder jetting, where deposited binder first creates a green shape.

Supporting detail: Addendum 14 — Readable process sources.

Polymer SLS and MJF select powder in different ways

Polymer SLS and MJF select powder in different ways

Selective laser sintering (SLS)
A laser scans selected regions of a polymer powder layer and thermally joins the particles. Unfused powder surrounds the parts in the stated process, so dedicated support structures are generally unnecessary; the build must cool before unpacking and depowdering.
Multi Jet Fusion (MJF)
A printhead places fusing and detailing agents on polymer powder, then applied heat fuses selected regions. The agents control fusion; they are not binder that leaves a green part for later sintering.

Both examples belong to PBF because powder is thermally fused during the build. Neither description proves that any polymer powder, color, wall, gap or enclosed cavity will work on a particular machine.

Loose powder can carry surrounding geometry during these stated polymer builds, but it must still be removed. A sealed hollow region can trap powder. An internal passage needs an accessible route for cleaning and inspection; “no dedicated supports” does not mean “no design constraints.”

Metal laser and electron-beam PBF need process-specific thermal reasoning

Metal laser and electron-beam PBF need process-specific thermal reasoning

The metal examples here use a laser or electron beam to melt or fuse selected regions of metal powder. The part develops through repeated melt-and-solidify events, so orientation and connection to the build system can affect heat flow, residual stress, distortion and later removal.

In a stated laser PBF case, sacrificial supports may anchor an overhang to the build plate and conduct heat away. Loose metal powder surrounding the part is not automatically an adequate thermal path. That does not create a universal rule that every metal PBF system and geometry needs the same supports.

Electron-beam PBF has process-specific strategies and exceptions. Current commercial examples can reduce or replace traditional supports for some parts. Record the exact machine, material, melt strategy, orientation and acceptance plan instead of transferring one support rule to every metal powder process.

Supporting detail: Addendum 15 — Why the support statement is qualified.

Design powder access and the post-build route with the part; Checklist; Practice

Design powder access and the post-build route with the part

  • Mark enclosed volumes, channels and lattice spaces; give loose powder a stated removal and inspection route.
  • State the material, machine/process variant, energy route and build orientation rather than writing only “PBF.”
  • Identify what supports geometry and, for the stated thermal case, what anchors the part and conducts heat.
  • Plan cooldown, unpacking, depowdering and any support removal before choosing inaccessible geometry.
  • List required postprocessing and inspection. A completed build is not automatically a qualified service part.

Material properties and acceptance depend on the qualified material-process-part route. Use Metals and Their Properties and Plastics as Materials for material foundations; use Heat Treating Metals only when a specified metal route actually calls for that operation.

Plan powder access Reason about a stated metal support Plan post-build acceptance

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

What Is Manufacturing?

Turn materials into useful products by choosing processes that fit the material, quantity, cost and required quality.

Manufacturing turns materials into useful products

Manufacturing turns materials into useful products

Manufacturing changes materials into parts and products people can use. A board becomes a shelf, plastic pellets become a bottle, and metal sheet becomes a bracket. Shape, properties, joints and surfaces all contribute to the result.

A process is an operation that makes one of those changes. Most products need several processes. A useful plan states what each operation must achieve and how the result will be checked.

Two organizing questions keep the subject manageable: What is the material? Use the four material families. What change are we making? Use the five process categories.

Primary processing makes usable material; secondary processing makes parts

Primary processing makes usable material; secondary processing makes parts

Primary processing converts raw resources into usable materials and common supply forms. Secondary processing turns those materials into parts or products. Stock means material supplied for further work, such as sheet, rod, boards or pellets.

Metal
Ore is refined into metal and made into stock such as sheet; sheet is then cut and bent into a bracket.
Plastic
Chemical feedstocks are made into polymer resin, often supplied as pellets; pellets are then molded into a bottle cap.
Wood
Logs are sawn into lumber; boards are then cut, joined and finished as furniture.
Glass
Mineral ingredients are melted and made into sheet glass; sheets are then cut and edge-finished for a window.

These terms describe a material's place in the supply chain. They do not replace the five process categories: sawing a log and sawing a furniture part are both separating.

Supporting detail: Addendum 16 — Why the boundary needs context.

Choose a process that fits material, quantity, cost and quality

Choose a process that fits material, quantity, cost and quality

Material
Can it tolerate the heat, force or chemical exposure? A process that bends metal sheet may crack a ceramic plate.
Quantity
A few parts favor flexible methods with little dedicated tooling. Repeated production can justify a mold or other tool made specifically for that part.
Cost
Count material, setup, tooling, labor, processing time, scrap and inspection. Cheap starting material can be expensive to turn into an acceptable part.
Required quality
Specify dimensions, allowable variation, strength and surface condition. Choose a route that can meet them consistently, then verify it.

For a small plastic cover, 3D printing may be useful for a few trial pieces; molding may suit repeated production after the design settles. Neither route wins from quantity alone: material behavior, geometry and acceptance requirements still matter.

Prototype, batch and mass production describe production situations, not universal numerical cutoffs. Manufacturing economics and design for manufacturing develop this comparison further.

Use Measurement Language to state dimensions clearly. 5S Workplace Organization explains how organized tools and materials support repeatable work.

Read every material unit through the same six-stage map

Read every material unit through the same six-stage map

Characteristics → Forming → Separating → Fabricating → Conditioning → Finishing

  1. Characteristics: What is the material like? Compare properties, useful forms and limitations.
  2. Forming: How can it take a shape?
  3. Separating: How can material be removed or cut apart?
  4. Fabricating: How can parts be joined?
  5. Conditioning: How can its internal properties be changed?
  6. Finishing: How can its surface be protected or improved?

This is the collection's learning map for the later plastics, wood and metals topics. Characteristics is the starting description, not a sixth process category.

The map is not a mandatory factory sequence. Wood may be dried before cutting; a metal part may be annealed between forming steps; some surfaces are finished before assembly. A product may repeat a category or omit one.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics

Choosing a Plastic Forming Process

Use geometry, material, quantity and tooling cost to narrow the process choice, then estimate cost per part and production rate.

Check geometry and material before comparing prices; Checklist

Check geometry and material before comparing prices

A low quoted price is irrelevant if the process cannot make the required shape or use the required material. Start with Plastics as Materials and the capability cards in Plastic Forming Processes.

  • Describe the geometry: hollow container, open sheet-like shell, constant cross-section or discrete solid part.
  • Choose a material type and candidate grade that meet the load, temperature and environment.
  • State the quantity, expected repeat orders and required delivery rate.
  • Check how the part leaves the tool: draft, undercuts and access to internal spaces.
  • Compare tooling, per-part cost, achievable detail and likely defects for the remaining processes.
Use part shape to build a short list; Practice

Use part shape to build a short list

Starting candidates, not exclusive rules
NeedStart withThen ask
Many thin-walled hollow containersBlow moldingCan the hot tube or preform stretch into this shape with an adequate wall?
A large hollow shell in a modest quantityRotational moldingAre the longer cycle and achievable detail acceptable?
An open tray or sheet-like coverThermoformingWill the sheet thin too much, and can it release from the tool?
A long constant cross-sectionExtrusionWhich end features or side holes would need later operations?
Many detailed discrete partsInjection moldingCan walls stay reasonably uniform, and does quantity justify the mold?
Repeated thermoset parts or composite panelsCompression moldingCan the charge fill the matched tools before curing?
A few detailed resin partsCastingWill mold life, trapped air and cure time meet the need?
A custom fiber-reinforced shellHand layupIs the labor acceptable, and can the reinforcement reach every region?

“Solid” does not mean “make every region thick.” An injection-molded housing is a discrete part, yet hollowing out bulky sections often improves it. Several processes can make a tank; size, quantity, resin and detail determine the better candidate.

Practice choosing a process

Spread tooling cost over the number of acceptable parts; Practice

Spread tooling cost over the number of acceptable parts

A simple comparison is average cost per part = tooling cost / quantity + variable cost per part. Variable cost includes the costs that grow with production, such as material and processing time. Tooling cost is paid even if only a few parts are made.

Illustrative estimates, not supplier prices: suppose two processes can both meet a cover's specification. Route A costs $900 for tooling and $14 per part. Route B costs $18,000 for tooling and $2 per part.

Average cost per acceptable part, assuming no scrap or extra charges
QuantityRoute ARoute B
100$900 / 100 + $14 = $23.00$18,000 / 100 + $2 = $182.00
5,000$900 / 5,000 + $14 = $14.18$18,000 / 5,000 + $2 = $5.60

Supporting detail: Addendum 17 — Find the quantity where the two estimates are equal.

Practice tooling cost per part Practice a cost crossover

Cycle time and cavity count set the ideal production rate; Practice

Cycle time and cavity count set the ideal production rate

A cavity makes one part per cycle. With cycle time in seconds, ideal parts per hour = 3600 / cycle time × cavities.

For a 30-second cycle and two identical cavities: 3600 / 30 × 2 = 240 parts/h. That assumes uninterrupted operation and every part acceptable. Use the complete repeating cycle time, including opening and ejection; do not add overlapping cooling time twice.

Actual useful output is lower when setup, stoppages or rejects occur. More cavities may increase tooling cost and require a larger machine, so a higher ideal rate does not by itself settle the process choice.

Practice production rate

Explain the choice with both a benefit and a limitation

Explain the choice with both a benefit and a limitation

A useful selection sounds like this: “For 300 large hollow PE garden reservoirs, investigate rotational molding because the shape fits and tooling can be economical at modest quantities. Confirm wall control and cycle time before committing.”

The quantity alone does not prove that choice. A narrow neck, precision sealing face, delivery deadline or different resin could change it. State the assumptions, identify a credible alternative, and compare the features that matter.

Supporting detail: Addendum 18 — Further process-selection reading.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics

Conditioning and Finishing Plastics

Separate property changes from surface treatments, and match annealing, smoothing and coatings to the exact plastic.

Conditioning changes properties; finishing changes the surface

Conditioning changes properties; finishing changes the surface

Conditioning changes the material's state or properties: relieving internal stress, developing a thermoset cure, or controlling absorbed moisture. Finishing changes the surface for appearance, protection or function. A part can need both. Removing a support is Separating; sanding the resulting surface is Finishing.

Start with the resin, dimensions and service requirement. A glossy surface does not prove that a part is strong, properly cured or dimensionally correct.

Annealing relieves stress, but can change dimensions

Annealing relieves stress, but can change dimensions

Annealing uses a controlled heating, holding and cooling schedule. In acrylic it can reduce stress left by machining, bending or polishing. It is not a general instruction to heat near molding temperature. Use the resin supplier's schedule for the grade and thickness, including support of the part during treatment.

Printed PLA can also be annealed. Depending on its formulation and thermal history, heating can allow more crystalline order and improve heat resistance. Shrinkage, expansion in another direction or warping can spoil a fit. Measure before and after; do not assume every strength property improves.

Supporting detail: Addendum 19 — Stress relief and crystallinity are different changes.

Curing creates a network; drying removes moisture

Curing creates a network; drying removes moisture

A thermoset cure is a chemical reaction that builds links between polymer chains. Resin and hardener, heat or light may initiate the reaction, depending on the system. Correct proportions, time and temperature matter. A prescribed post-cure can develop properties further; an already cured thermoset will not simply remelt like a thermoplastic.

Drying moisture-sensitive filament addresses a different problem. Moisture can affect extrusion and part quality, but drying does not replace annealing or cure. Use a drying schedule intended for the material; excessive heat can deform filament or its spool.

Supporting detail: Addendum 20 — Other ways processors change plastic properties.

Remove scratches progressively before adding gloss or paint

Remove scratches progressively before adding gloss or paint

Sanding replaces a coarse scratch pattern with progressively finer scratches. Start with the finest abrasive that will remove the defect efficiently. Within the same grit system, a larger number generally means a finer abrasive. A sequence such as P240 → P320 → P400 → P600 illustrates progression; it is not a required recipe for every plastic or coating.

Remove the previous scratch pattern before moving on and clean away abrasive residue between stages. Wet sanding with suitable waterproof abrasive can reduce loading and heat where the material and equipment permit it. Keep corners and fit surfaces from rounding over. Paint may need a controlled scuffed surface rather than a polished one; follow its preparation specification.

Tumbling can finish many parts together, but media and time affect edge rounding and small features. Buffing can improve gloss, but excessive heat or pressure can smear the surface. Check a representative sample rather than equating more polishing with a better part.

Flame and solvent smoothing are material-specific processes

Flame and solvent smoothing are material-specific processes

Flame polishing can smooth suitable acrylic edges by briefly softening the surface. It can also round edges and introduce stress. It is not a general treatment for clear plastics: polycarbonate is not interchangeable with acrylic, and a process must be validated for its exact grade. A clear edge is not necessarily an optically accurate or low-stress edge.

Solvent or vapor smoothing softens a compatible polymer's surface chemically. Acetone smoothing is associated with ABS and ASA; do not transfer that recipe to PLA or PETG. Smoothing can erase fine lettering, change dimensions and alter mechanical performance. It does not guarantee that weak layer bonds inside a print have been repaired.

These descriptions explain process selection, not operating procedures. Refer to Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets, Fire Safety and Equipment Operating Procedure for the relevant controls.

Supporting detail: Addendum 21 — Why a clear surface can crack later.

Coatings need adhesion as well as the right appearance; Practice

Coatings need adhesion as well as the right appearance

For paint, remove contamination with a compatible cleaner, prepare the surface as specified and use a primer or adhesion promoter when the coating system calls for one. PE and PP often need special preparation or products because of low surface energy. A primer is not automatically compatible with every plastic. Trial the complete system, including cure, on a representative sample.

Dip coating deposits a liquid film as the part is withdrawn, followed by drying or curing as the formulation requires. Withdrawal rate and liquid properties affect thickness. Powder coating plastics requires a suitable way to attract or deposit the powder and a cure that the part can withstand; an insulating plastic does not become conductive merely because a grounding wire touches it.

Electroplating needs a conductive surface. Plastics therefore require preparation and a conductive layer before electroplating. Decorative options also include printing, decals, in-mold labels and dyes for receptive polymers. Choose them for the required abrasion, outdoor exposure and chemical resistance; decoration is not automatically protection.

Supporting detail: Addendum 22 — Powder coating needs a complete substrate and cure system.

Practice choosing a finish

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics

Cutting and Machining Plastics

Choose a separating process for the plastic and the feature, then control heat, chips and edge damage.

Choose the cut from the material and the feature

Choose the cut from the material and the feature

Separating removes material. A saw makes a blank, a drill makes a round hole, and a router or mill can make an outline, pocket or slot. Identify the resin and grade before choosing the process: two clear sheets can be acrylic and polycarbonate, with very different cutting behavior.

ProcessUseful forWhat controls the result
SawingStraight cuts or curved blanks on a band sawUse a blade intended for the plastic and thickness. Teeth must cut without grabbing or packing the cut with chips; the finest tooth spacing is not always best.
DrillingHoles through sheet or solid stockUse suitable drill geometry, support the exit surface and provide chip clearance. Brittle acrylic can crack when the drill grabs at breakthrough.
Milling and routingAccurate edges, slots and pocketsSharp cutting edges, room for chips to escape and a supported workpiece reduce melting and chatter.
Laser cuttingSheet profiles in an approved materialThe resin, additives, thickness and laser wavelength matter. A glossy edge alone does not prove dimensional accuracy.
Hot-wire cuttingContours in suitable thermoplastic foamA heated wire softens a narrow path. This is not a general cutting method for solid plastic sheet or every foam formulation.

See Milling Operations for tool paths and feature access. Machine use belongs with Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping.

Make chips instead of rubbing the plastic hot

Make chips instead of rubbing the plastic hot

Heat builds up near the cut because plastics generally conduct heat poorly. Softened chips can stick to the tool or weld back onto the edge. The symptoms are smeared surfaces, strings of softened material and chips packed into the cutter.

Slowing the feed alone can make melting worse. Feed is how quickly the tool advances through the work; spindle speed is how quickly it turns. Too little advance per tooth lets the edge rub instead of taking a useful chip. Start with cutting data for the resin and tool, keep the tool sharp, and maintain chip clearance. Reducing excessive spindle speed may help, but feed, speed and cut depth must be considered together.

Deep holes need a planned way to clear chips. Coolants and cleaners must be compatible with the plastic; an unsuitable liquid can cause fine cracks called crazing. Use Feeds and Speeds for the relationships, not its metal cutting values as plastic settings.

Supporting detail: Addendum 23 — Why a slower cut can produce more heat.

Acrylic, PVC and polycarbonate behave differently under a laser

Acrylic, PVC and polycarbonate behave differently under a laser

Acrylic (PMMA) absorbs the infrared energy of a CO₂ laser. Concentrated heating removes material along the cut and can leave a smooth, glossy edge. That result depends on the sheet grade, thickness and process settings; it is not a promise for every clear plastic or every laser.

PVC is not a laser-cutting substitute for acrylic. Heating PVC can release hydrogen chloride; with moisture it forms hydrochloric acid, creating an exposure and corrosion concern. This is a chemical incompatibility, not simply a poor-looking edge.

Polycarbonate is often a poor choice for a clean CO₂-laser-cut sheet edge. It can yellow, char and leave a degraded edge instead of acrylic's clear finish. Specialized processes can cut some polycarbonate, so “polycarbonate cannot be laser processed” is too broad. Routing or sawing is often the better starting choice for a clear polycarbonate profile. Do not assign PVC's chlorine chemistry to polycarbonate.

Material approval and operating controls belong with Equipment Operating Procedure and Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets. Appearance or a trade name is not enough to identify an unknown sheet.

Supporting detail: Addendum 24 — Manufacturer references and the limits of a material list.

Trim the molding excess without cutting into the part; Practice

Trim the molding excess without cutting into the part

A gate is the entry from a molding flow channel into the part cavity. Degating separates the part from that feed connection. Flash is a thin unwanted fin, often at a mold joint; trimming removes it. A burr is a raised edge left by cutting. These are different defects, even when the same trimming tool can remove them.

Support the part near the cut and leave the required contour intact. Cutting into the wall creates a notch that may start a crack. For batches, tumbling with suitable media can remove small burrs, but it can also round wanted edges or damage thin features. Inspect the dimensions and surface after the trial.

Practice diagnosing a melted cut

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics

FDM 3D Printing

Read an FDM part as deposited roads and layers, then choose orientation, walls, infill and supports for its job.

A slicer turns a solid model into deposited layers

A slicer turns a solid model into deposited layers

Material extrusion is the standard family in which material is selectively dispensed through a nozzle. This page covers thermoplastic filament printing, often called fused filament fabrication (FFF). Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is a registered trademark of Stratasys for an implementation of this mechanism. The machine feeds filament into a heated nozzle and lays down narrow roads of softened material that bond as the part builds. Relative motion between the nozzle and build plate advances the layers; the nozzle itself does not have to move upward on every printer.

A slicer converts the model into tool paths, including walls, internal fill and any temporary supports. Preview those paths before printing. An enclosed shape on a CAD screen does not tell you how its underside will be supported.

Compare material extrusion with the other standard routes in Additive Manufacturing Process Families.

Supporting detail: Addendum 25 — Where additive manufacturing fits the five course categories.

Layer height, walls and infill do different jobs

Layer height, walls and infill do different jobs

Layer height is the vertical increment between layers. A smaller height makes steps on sloping surfaces finer and usually adds print time. It does not make all small horizontal features printable: nozzle size, road width and motion accuracy also matter.

Walls or perimeters trace the boundary. Top and bottom layers close the part. Infill is the pattern inside those boundaries. More infill generally adds material and time, but strength also depends on walls, orientation, bonding and load direction. A 20% infill setting does not mean the entire part uses 20% of its solid volume, because the walls and skins remain.

Simple layer-count example: for a 24 mm height with every layer 0.20 mm thick, 24 ÷ 0.20 = 120 layers. Real slicers may use a different first-layer height or variable layers. Halving layer height roughly doubles the layer count, not necessarily the total print time.

Orient for the load as well as for fewer supports; Checklist

Orient for the load as well as for fewer supports

FDM parts are anisotropic: properties depend on direction. A load that pulls layers apart can expose a weaker bond than a load carried along continuous deposited roads. Avoid placing the main tensile load across layer interfaces when an orientation can carry it along the layers. This is a design starting point, not a strength rating.

An overhang extends beyond the layer below. A short bridge spans between supported ends. A long unsupported underside may need temporary support material. Support contacts can leave marks, so keep them away from critical visible or mating surfaces where possible. There is no universal overhang angle that works for all materials and settings.

For a rectangular test bar pulled along its length, laying its length in the build plane usually gives a better starting orientation than standing it upright and pulling across stacked layers. A bracket may have several important load directions; choose a compromise or change the design, then test it.

  • Mark the main load direction and critical fit surfaces on the model.
  • Compare orientations for layer direction, build-plate contact and unsupported undersides.
  • Preview walls, infill and supports one layer at a time.
  • Check that support can actually be removed from each enclosed space.
Choose filament for service conditions and printer capability

Choose filament for service conditions and printer capability

FilamentUseful starting pointCheck before choosing
PLAStiff models and easy-to-print prototypesHeat exposure and impact requirements; a neat print is not automatically suitable for a warm enclosure.
PETGTougher functional parts with useful layer bondingStringing, moisture and support-removal behavior for the grade.
ABS / ASAApplications needing greater heat resistance than ordinary PLA; ASA is often chosen for outdoor exposureWarping control, equipment capability and processing requirements.
TPUFlexible partsHardness grade and whether the feed system can handle flexible filament.
Nylon (polyamide)Tough engineering partsMoisture control, dimensional change and the required printing conditions.

PVA is used as a water-soluble support material in compatible multi-material systems; it is not a universal companion for every filament. Use the exact filament manufacturer's settings and the printer's limits. Consult Equipment Operating Procedure and Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets for process controls.

Supporting detail: Addendum 26 — Material guidance is grade-specific.

Estimate mass from deposited volume, not infill alone; Practice

Estimate mass from deposited volume, not infill alone

Mass = deposited volume × density. If a simplified model has 8 cm³ of solid walls and skins plus a 32 cm³ interior at 25% infill, its estimated deposited volume is 8 + (32 × 0.25) = 16 cm³. At an assumed density of 1.24 g/cm³, that is 19.84 g. Supports, brims and purge material add more.

This estimate treats infill percentage as a volume fraction of the interior. A slicer estimates the actual paths more closely. Time also includes travel, acceleration, heating and cooling constraints; volume alone does not give an exact printing duration.

Post-processing choices are in Conditioning and Finishing Plastics. Practice estimating filament mass

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics

Joining Plastics

Match solvent cement, adhesive, welding or mechanical joints to the plastic pair, load and need for disassembly.

Start with both plastics and what the joint must do; Checklist

Start with both plastics and what the joint must do

Fabricating joins pieces into a useful assembly. Name both materials, then state the load, service temperature, appearance and whether the assembly must come apart. A leak-tight seam, a removable cover and a clear display corner need different joints.

  • Identify the two resins and any coating or surface contamination.
  • State the load direction, environment and need for disassembly or sealing.
  • Check the joining product or process guidance for that material pair.
  • Make a representative trial joint and inspect it after full cure or cooling.
Solvent cement softens the surfaces; adhesive adds a bond layer

Solvent cement softens the surfaces; adhesive adds a bond layer

Solvent cementing uses a compatible liquid to soften or dissolve the surfaces so polymer chains can mix across the joint. As solvent leaves, the joint develops strength. It is chemical softening, not heat melting. Acrylic-to-acrylic is a common application; PVC and ABS also have specific cement systems. The cement must match the resin and fit of the joint.

Adhesives bond through a separate layer. Epoxies, cyanoacrylates and other formulations have different gap, flexibility and temperature limits. “Plastic glue” does not mean it bonds every plastic. Allow the specified cure time before loading; a joint that holds itself together may not have reached service strength.

Polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) resist many ordinary adhesives. Their low surface energy makes it difficult for an adhesive to spread into intimate contact, called wetting. Specialized adhesives or a controlled surface treatment can help; sanding alone is not a universal fix. See Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets for chemical handling.

Supporting detail: Addendum 27 — Why a clean-looking bond can peel off.

Welding needs compatible thermoplastics and a designed joint

Welding needs compatible thermoplastics and a designed joint

Plastic welding heats the joint region so compatible thermoplastics can fuse. Cooling while the joint is held in position completes the connection. Cured thermosets do not remelt into a comparable fusion weld. Even two thermoplastics are not automatically weld-compatible.

MethodHow the joint formsTypical reason to choose it
Hot-gas weldingA controlled stream of heated gas softens the joint faces and compatible filler rod.Accessible seams or repairs in weldable sheet.
Extrusion weldingA tool supplies molten compatible filler while the base surfaces are preheated.Larger seams needing more deposited material than a small rod weld.
Hot-plate weldingA heated tool softens mating faces; the tool withdraws and the faces are pressed together.Parts with accessible matching joint faces.
Hot-wire or resistance-element weldingElectrical resistance heats a wire or element at a designed joint region. Tool arrangements differ.A localized joint designed for that heating arrangement; not the foam-cutting process.
Ultrasonic weldingA horn applies rapid mechanical vibration under force, generating heat at the joint.Repeated assembly of compatible molded parts with a suitable joint geometry.
Heat sealingHeat and pressure fuse compatible film surfaces or their sealant layers.Bag and packaging seams; not every multilayer film seals to itself.

Supporting detail: Addendum 28 — Why heat alone does not guarantee a strong or sealed weld.

Hot-melt adhesive is not a fusion weld

Hot-melt adhesive is not a fusion weld

A hot-melt adhesive is applied molten and usually gains handling strength as it cools. The adhesive melts; the two parts do not have to melt together. Choose the formulation for both surfaces, the available assembly time and the service temperature. An ordinary hot-melt joint may soften or creep under sustained load in warmth. Fast setting is not the same as suitability for structural service.

Use mechanical joints when access and disassembly matter; Practice

Use mechanical joints when access and disassembly matter

A snap fit bends a feature during assembly so it catches behind another feature. It needs room to flex, rounded transitions and a resin that tolerates the required strain. Some snap fits release repeatedly; others are intentionally difficult to undo.

Thread-forming screws for plastics create their mating thread in a designed hole. Repeated removal can wear plastic threads. A threaded insert supplies a metal thread; a heat-set insert is installed by locally softening a thermoplastic around it. Hole size, surrounding wall thickness and installation conditions come from the insert supplier. A metal insert cannot rescue an undersized plastic wall.

Through-bolts and suitable washers can spread the clamping load. Excessive tightening can crack brittle plastic; sustained load can cause creep, a gradual change in shape, and reduce clamping force. Allow for movement and thermal expansion rather than trapping a sheet tightly at every hole.

Compare two cases: a clear permanent acrylic corner is a candidate for compatible solvent cement; a PP cover that must be removed regularly is a candidate for screws and a suitable thread arrangement. An adhesive that works on the first pair tells you little about the second.

Supporting detail: Addendum 29 — Insert dimensions come from the chosen insert system.

Practice choosing a removable joint

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics

Plastic Forming Processes

How eight plastic and composite processes shape material, what they can make, and where tooling and geometry limit the choice.

Start with the shape and how the material becomes solid

Start with the shape and how the material becomes solid

These processes make a shape by moving softened material, stretching sheet or curing resin in tooling. A mold shapes a part against its surfaces; a die gives flowing material a cross-section. Tooling is the equipment made specifically to produce the part.

Use the process-category foundations topic for the five-category framework. Here, follow what happens to the material: thermoplastics usually set by cooling; thermosets set by curing. Review Plastics as Materials if that distinction is unclear.

For equipment operation and hazards, use the Safety collection's Equipment Operating Procedure, Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets topics.

Injection molding fills a closed cavity, then repeats the cycle

Injection molding fills a closed cavity, then repeats the cycle

In conventional thermoplastic injection molding, a heated barrel and screw prepare the melt. The screw advances to push a measured shot (the material delivered in one injection) through a nozzle into a clamped mold.

  1. Clamp: close the mold and hold it against the pressure of the incoming melt.
  2. Inject: fill the cavity.
  3. Hold/pack: maintain pressure to feed additional material as it shrinks, while the gate can still pass melt.
  4. Cool: allow enough heat to leave for the part to keep its shape during removal.
  5. Eject: open the mold and push the part free, commonly with ejector pins. Close for the next cycle.

Materials and products: thermoplastics such as ABS, PP and nylon become housings, caps, clips and gears. Specialized injection systems also mold thermosets; those require curing, so the cooling-based cycle above is not universal.

Tooling and quantity: detailed, pressure-resistant molds are a substantial initial investment. Repeated cycles and multiple cavities can make the investment worthwhile for many identical parts.

Supporting detail: Addendum 30 — See the machine and cycle in a public explainer.

Sprue, runner and gate carry melt into the part

Sprue, runner and gate carry melt into the part

In a conventional sprue-and-runner layout, the sprue receives melt from the nozzle, a runner distributes it, and a gate is the restricted entrance to a part cavity. One mold may contain several cavities, and one cavity may have several gates.

Draft is a slight taper on a surface in the mold-opening direction. It helps the part release instead of scraping along the tool. Injection molding can produce ribs, bosses (raised features around holes) and fine detail, but every feature must have a way out of the mold.

An undercut traps material behind a tool feature. It may require a moving side core, another special mechanism or a redesigned part. A simple two-part mold cannot produce every enclosed hollow shape.

Uniform walls reduce sink marks and uneven shrinkage; Practice

Uniform walls reduce sink marks and uneven shrinkage

Aim for a reasonably uniform wall thickness, with gradual transitions where thickness must change. A thick mass cools differently from an adjacent thin wall. Its shrinkage can pull the surface inward, leaving a sink mark, or contribute to distortion.

A solid block under a thin housing wall is therefore a warning sign. Hollow out the bulky region where possible and use appropriately sized ribs for support. Packing and cooling settings also matter; changing the drawing is not the only remedy.

Supporting detail: Addendum 31 — Three design clues to recognize.

Practice mold design problems

Blow molding inflates a hot tube or preform into a hollow part

Blow molding inflates a hot tube or preform into a hollow part

A mold closes around a hot parison (tube), or a previously molded preform. Air pressure expands the material against the mold, then it cools. Extrusion blow molding starts with a tube; injection-based versions start with a molded preform.

Materials and products: thermoplastics; HDPE detergent bottles and PET beverage bottles are familiar examples made by different blow-molding variants.

Tooling and quantity: dedicated molds and machinery favor repeated production, especially large packaging runs. Mold complexity and the chosen variant affect cost; lower forming pressure does not make the whole production line inexpensive.

Geometry: good for thin-walled hollow containers. Stretching affects wall thickness; external detail is controlled better than internal detail. It does not directly make a solid gear or complex internal ribs. Mold parting lines, and pinch-off seams in extrusion-blown parts, may remain visible.

Supporting detail: Addendum 32 — Public process reference.

Rotational molding coats a mold to make a large hollow shell

Rotational molding coats a mold to make a large hollow shell

A measured charge, usually thermoplastic powder, goes inside a mold. Heating and slow rotation about two axes distribute material over the inside surface as it melts. The mold keeps moving during cooling before the shell is removed.

Materials and products: predominantly polyethylene; tanks, playground shells and kayaks.

Tooling and quantity: molds do not withstand injection pressure, so tooling is often less costly for a large part. Heating and cooling the mold takes time, making low-to-medium quantities attractive compared with faster processes.

Geometry: large hollow parts with relatively even walls are a strength. Local thickness, corners and fine tolerances still need care. Tiny details, very thin walls and solid precision parts are poor fits. This is slow coating of the mold, not high-speed centrifugal casting.

Supporting detail: Addendum 33 — Public process reference.

Thermoforming stretches a sheet into a tray or shell

Thermoforming stretches a sheet into a tray or shell

Heat thermoplastic sheet until it is pliable, form it against a tool, cool it and trim the edge. In vacuum forming, removing air between sheet and tool lets outside air pressure press the sheet against the tool. Pressure forming adds pressure on the other side.

Materials and products: thermoplastic sheets such as PETG, ABS and polystyrene; packaging trays, display covers and equipment liners.

Tooling and quantity: a simple one-sided tool can suit prototypes or short runs. Durable tools and automated equipment also support very large packaging volumes.

Geometry: best for open, sheet-like shapes with draft. Deep draws stretch and thin the sheet; the tool controls one surface most directly. It cannot create a solid boss or a closed bottle from one sheet in this basic process. Undercuts complicate release.

Supporting detail: Addendum 34 — Public process reference.

Extrusion makes a continuous, constant cross-section

Extrusion makes a continuous, constant cross-section

A screw moves and melts plastic, then pushes it continuously through a shaped die. Cooling and sizing equipment establish the final dimensions. The product is cut to length or wound.

Materials and products: commonly thermoplastics such as PVC and PE; pipe, tubing, sheet, film and window profiles.

Tooling and quantity: a profile die is often simpler than a complex injection mold, but the production line and setup still cost money. Long runs spread those costs over many meters of product.

Geometry: the die can make solid or hollow cross-sections. It cannot directly put a cap on the end of a tube or create isolated holes along one side; those require other operations. A long product with the same section everywhere is the main clue.

Supporting detail: Addendum 35 — Public process reference.

Compression molding presses a charge between matched tools

Compression molding presses a charge between matched tools

Place a measured amount of material in an open mold. Closing the heated tool applies pressure and spreads the charge into shape. With a thermosetting compound, the part cures before removal; cooling alone is not what hardens it.

Materials and products: often thermosets or fiber-filled thermosetting compounds; electrical components and composite body panels. Thermoplastic sheet composites can also be compression molded, with a cooling-based solidification step.

Tooling and quantity: matched tools and a press require investment, often justified by repeated medium-to-high production. Tooling is not automatically cheap; size, surface quality and precision matter.

Geometry: both faces can be shaped, including ribs and shaped panels. Material must flow before it cures; extremely thin features, deep narrow details and trapped undercuts are difficult.

Supporting detail: Addendum 36 — Public process reference.

Casting fills a mold with liquid resin for small quantities

Casting fills a mold with liquid resin for small quantities

Liquid resin fills a mold and hardens. In common small-batch resin casting, mixed components react and cure. A flexible mold made from a master pattern can reproduce surface detail.

Materials and products: often thermosets such as epoxy, polyurethane or unsaturated polyester; prototypes, decorative replicas and electrical encapsulation. Casting is broader than polyurethane casting; some cast plastics, such as cast acrylic, are thermoplastic after polymerization.

Tooling and quantity: flexible molds can have a low initial cost but limited life. Labor and cure time make this useful for short runs rather than a default for millions of pieces.

Geometry: good detail and some undercuts are possible with flexible tooling. Trapped air, cure shrinkage and heat from the reaction limit thin passages and thick pours. A closed hollow space still needs a removable or sacrificial core, or a different casting method.

Supporting detail: Addendum 37 — Public process reference.

Hand layup builds a fiber-reinforced composite against a tool

Hand layup builds a fiber-reinforced composite against a tool

In wet hand layup, reinforcing fabric or mat is placed against a mold, wetted with liquid resin and consolidated to reduce trapped air. Layers build thickness, then the resin cures.

Materials and products: usually a thermosetting polyester or epoxy matrix with glass or carbon fibers; boat shells and custom covers. These are composites in the Wood & Composites material family. Prepreg layup uses reinforcement already containing resin and is a related but different route.

Tooling and quantity: relatively simple one-sided molds support small runs and large custom parts. Manual work and cure time limit production rate.

Geometry: good for broad shells. The mold gives one face its finish; the other depends on the layup. Tight corners, inaccessible cavities and precise thickness on both faces are difficult. Fiber direction affects strength, so layer arrangement is part of the design.

Supporting detail: Addendum 38 — Public process reference.

Apply these comparisons in Choosing a Plastic Forming Process. Plastic separating, fabricating, 3D printing and finishing are separate topics; for the general milling process, see Milling Operations.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics

Plastics as Materials

Polymer chains, thermoplastics and thermosets, common plastics, and what resin identification codes actually tell you.

Plastics get their behavior from polymer chains

Plastics get their behavior from polymer chains

A polymer is a substance made of very large molecules built from repeating units. Small starting molecules called monomers react to build those molecules. Many polymers have long chains; some also have branches or chemical links between chains.

A plastic combines a polymer with ingredients that may change its color, flexibility, processing behavior or resistance to weather. The polymer name is a starting point, not a complete material specification. Two grades of the same plastic can behave differently.

Plastics is one of the four material families in the material-family foundations topic. A polymer reinforced with glass or carbon fibers is a composite; the course places composites in Wood & Composites.

Thermoplastics soften again; cured thermosets do not remelt

Thermoplastics soften again; cured thermosets do not remelt

The useful distinction is behavior on reheating
TypeWhat happensExamples and recycling
ThermoplasticHeating makes the material soft enough to reshape or flow. Cooling makes it firm again. Reheating can repeat this change, within the material's processing limits.PE, PP, PVC, PLA, ABS, PETG, acrylic, polycarbonate and nylon. Clean, compatible material can often be remelted for recycling; contamination, degradation and available collection systems limit actual recovery.
ThermosetCuring forms a network of chemical links between molecules. The cured material cannot be melted back into a moldable liquid. Excessive heating degrades it.Cured epoxy and unsaturated polyester resin. They cannot be recycled by ordinary melt-and-remold processing; specialized recovery methods may exist.

Curing is a chemical change; cooling is a temperature change. A two-part epoxy becoming solid is not simply a hot plastic cooling down.

Supporting detail: Addendum 39 — Softening, melting and heat resistance are different questions.

Light weight and corrosion resistance come with limits

Light weight and corrosion resistance come with limits

  • Light weight: many unfilled plastics have much lower density than metals. Low weight does not automatically mean high stiffness.
  • Chemical resistance: plastics do not rust like steel, but a chemical may soften, swell or crack a particular plastic. Check the material, chemical, temperature and exposure time together.
  • Low softening or melting temperatures: many common thermoplastics are easy to form with heat but unsuitable for hot, loaded service.
  • Creep: slow deformation under a sustained load. A plastic shelf can keep sagging even when its load stays constant.
  • UV degradation: sunlight can discolor or embrittle susceptible grades. Outdoor service calls for a suitable resin and stabilization, not just a preferred color.
  • Electrical insulation: many unfilled plastics resist current flow. Conductive fillers and special formulations can change that behavior.

Supporting detail: Addendum 40 — Why a short strength test does not settle a long service life.

Match common thermoplastics to their useful properties

Match common thermoplastics to their useful properties

These are typical uses and tradeoffs, not design ratings for every grade. All materials in this table are thermoplastics.

Common plastics: a first selection, followed by a grade data sheet
MaterialTypical uses and strengthsWatch for
PLA — polylactic acidModels, packaging and filament; stiff, often made from renewable feedstocks.Ordinary grades have limited heat resistance and can be brittle. Bio-based does not mean an item belongs in home compost or a recycling bin.
ABS — acrylonitrile butadiene styreneHousings and toys; a useful balance of toughness and rigidity.Ordinary grades weather poorly outdoors; some solvents attack it.
PETG — glycol-modified PETClear displays, formed packaging and filament; tough and readily thermoformed.Scratches and limited service temperature. PETG is not interchangeable with bottle-grade PET.
Acrylic / PMMA — polymethyl methacrylateSigns, displays and glazing; clarity, stiffness and good weathering.More prone to cracking under impact than polycarbonate; vulnerable to some solvents.
PC — polycarbonateImpact-resistant glazing and housings; transparent and tough.Scratching and chemical attack; select an appropriate UV-resistant grade for outdoor exposure.
HDPE — high-density polyethyleneBottles, tanks and pipe; tough with useful chemical resistance.Low stiffness compared with metals, creep and substantial thermal expansion.
LDPE — low-density polyethyleneFilm and squeeze bottles; flexible and tough.Less stiff than HDPE and limited temperature capability.
PP — polypropyleneContainers, caps and living hinges (thin flexible connections); light and chemically resistant.Creep, UV sensitivity in unstabilized grades and reduced toughness in cold service.
PVC — polyvinyl chlorideRigid pipe and window profiles; plasticized grades make flexible tubing and cable insulation.Properties depend strongly on additives; limited temperature range.
Nylon / PA — polyamideGears, bearings and cable ties; strength, toughness and wear resistance.Absorbed moisture changes dimensions and mechanical properties.

Supporting detail: Addendum 41 — Material references for checking a particular choice.

Epoxy and polyester resin cure into thermosets

Epoxy and polyester resin cure into thermosets

Two common thermosetting resin systems
ResinTypical uses and strengthsLimitations
EpoxyAdhesives, cast parts and composite matrices; good adhesion and generally low cure shrinkage.Mixing and cure conditions affect properties. Often costs more than general-purpose polyester resin; unprotected epoxy can degrade in sunlight.
Unsaturated polyester resinFiberglass boat shells and panels; economical for many composite parts.Typically greater cure shrinkage and lower adhesive performance than epoxy. Cured resin cannot be remelted.

“Polyester” alone is ambiguous. PET packaging is a thermoplastic polyester. The unsaturated polyester resin used in a conventional fiberglass layup cures into a thermoset. See the hand-layup card in Plastic Forming Processes.

Supporting detail: Addendum 42 — Where the resin comparison comes from.

Resin codes identify plastic; they do not promise recycling; Practice

Resin codes identify plastic; they do not promise recycling

The number on a container is a resin identification code (RIC). It can help sorting, but it does not say whether the local recycling program accepts that product.

The seven code-to-resin matches, checked against current public guidance
CodePlastic
1 — PET / PETEPolyethylene terephthalate
2 — HDPEHigh-density polyethylene
3 — PVCPolyvinyl chloride (vinyl)
4 — LDPELow-density polyethylene
5 — PPPolypropylene
6 — PSPolystyrene
7 — OTHERResins outside the first six categories; also some combinations of resins. It is not one particular plastic.

For example, code 5 identifies PP; it does not prove that a PP lid is accepted with PP containers. Use the collector's instructions for that item. Do not assign PETG to code 1 just because its name contains PET.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Composites

Fiber Direction and Elastic Stiffness

Predict how one unidirectional composite layer stretches and skews when its fibers turn relative to the same applied stress.

Fiber direction changes elastic response

Fiber direction changes elastic response

A fiber-reinforced composite combines a reinforcement with a surrounding matrix. In a unidirectional layer, the reinforcement is continuous and parallel. The layer is much stiffer along the fibers than across them, so its elastic response depends on direction.

Stress is force divided by loaded area. This lesson compares patches under the same uniform axial stress, so each square millimeter carries the same applied force. Strain is deformation divided by original dimension. Elastic stiffness connects stress to strain in the reversible small-strain model.

The illustrative material uses E1 = 40 GPa along the fibers, E2 = 10 GPa across them, G12 = 5 GPa, and ν12 = 0.30. These round teaching values do not describe a named composite and are not design allowables.

Review Plastics as Materials for reinforcement, matrix, thermosets, and thermoplastics. Review Plastic Forming Processes for hand layup and other forming routes.

Predict the least stretch, then turn the fibers; Interactive

Predict the least stretch, then turn the fibers

Read the directions: the fiber angle is the starting, unloaded direction measured from the horizontal load axis. In this drawing, +45° slopes up to the right and −45° slopes down to the right. Axial means along the load; transverse means across it. The drawn fibers follow the exaggerated deformation, so their visible slope can differ from the starting angle on the control.

Predict first: identical free material patches carry uniform axial stress σx = 10 MPa, with no applied transverse or shear stress. Which orientation stretches least: 0°, 45°, or 90°?

Same illustrative lamina and same 10 MPa stress
Fiber angleEffective axial stiffnessAxial strainTransverse strainEngineering shear strain
0°40.00 GPa0.0250%−0.0075%0 µε
+45°12.90 GPa0.0775%−0.0225%−375 µε
−45°12.90 GPa0.0775%−0.0225%+375 µε
90°10.00 GPa0.1000%−0.0075%0 µε

Result: 0° stretches least because the stiff fiber direction is aligned with the load. Opposite 45° angles have the same axial stiffness and stretch, but their shear strain has opposite sign.

This is a freely deforming material patch loaded by uniform edge traction. It is not a tensile-test coupon held in rigid grips: grips would restrain the off-axis skew and create another boundary-value problem.

Off-axis extension can also create shear strain

Off-axis extension can also create shear strain

At 0° and 90°, the loading direction matches a principal material direction. The patch stretches and narrows without extension–shear coupling. At an off-axis angle, an axial stress can also make the free patch skew. Turning +45° to −45° mirrors that skew while leaving the axial stiffness unchanged.

The interactive drawing exaggerates every strain by the same factor of 120. A larger drawn change therefore means a larger calculated strain; the display does not secretly rescale each angle to fill the frame.

Supporting detail: Addendum 44 — How the axial stiffness is calculated.

Stiffness does not predict strength; Practice

Stiffness does not predict strength

A smaller strain under the same stress means greater elastic stiffness. It does not say when the material fails, which direction is safest, or which laminate should be built. Strength needs failure data and criteria; a laminate also needs its complete stacking sequence, ply thicknesses, bonding, environment, loading, and boundary conditions.

This lesson models one thin, continuous-fiber lamina in small-strain linear elasticity and plane stress. It omits failure, damage, buckling, bending, temperature, moisture, manufacturing defects, grips, and interaction between multiple plies.

Supporting detail: Addendum 45 — Primary mechanics source and model boundary.

Practice axial strain Practice angle symmetry Practice model limits

Stack plies into a laminate and find one equally stiff in every direction; Interactive

Stack plies into a laminate and find one equally stiff in every direction

A real part is rarely one ply. A laminate is a stack of bonded plies, each with its own fiber angle. The stacking sequence is written from the top face down: [0/90] is a 0° ply on top of a 90° ply, and a subscript s means the list is mirrored about the midplane, so [0/90]s is [0/90/90/0]. Every ply here is the same illustrative ply as the card above, 0.125 mm thick.

Challenge: using only 0°, +45°, −45° and 90° plies, build a laminate that is equally stiff in every in-plane direction. Then find out why an unsymmetric stack curls when it is pulled.

Same illustrative plies, 0.125 mm each. Ex is flat-held (curvature held at zero).
Stack (top first)SymmetricBalancedQuasi-isotropicEx at 0° / 45° / 90°, GPaLargest |Bij|
[0]yesyesno40.00 / 12.90 / 10.000
[0/90]noyesno25.21 / 14.82 / 25.21239.8 N
[0/90]syesyesno25.21 / 14.82 / 25.210
[+45/−45]noyesno14.82 / 25.21 / 14.82119.9 N
[±45]syesyesno14.82 / 25.21 / 14.820
[0/+45/−45/90]syesyesyes20.74 / 20.74 / 20.740

A single 0° ply gives 40.00 GPa along x and 10.00 GPa along y, the fiber-orientation result for the same ply.

The polar plot is a stiffness rose. Its radius in each direction is the laminate's effective in-plane modulus Ex(θ) for a pull in that direction, computed with the laminate held flat. A circle means the same in-plane stiffness every way.

Symmetric, balanced and quasi-isotropic are three different properties

Symmetric, balanced and quasi-isotropic are three different properties

  • Symmetric: the plies above the midplane are a mirror image of the plies below it. Then the coupling matrix B is zero, so in-plane loads and bending stay separate. [0/90]s is symmetric; [0/90] is not.
  • Balanced: every +θ ply has a −θ ply of the same thickness somewhere in the stack (0° and 90° plies need no partner). Then A16 = A26 = 0: there is no extension–shear coupling in the flat-held in-plane response, so a pull along x or y held flat does not shear the laminate in its plane. A balanced and symmetric stack also has B = 0, so it does not shear when free either; a balanced unsymmetric stack such as [0/+45/−45/90] can still shear and twist when free to curve.
  • Quasi-isotropic: the in-plane stiffness matrix A is the same in every direction, so the rose is a circle. Equal numbers of 0°, +45°, −45° and 90° plies do this, and because A ignores the order of the plies, [0/+45/−45/90]s and [+45/0/−45/90]s both qualify. It describes in-plane stiffness only; bending stiffness D still depends on order and direction.

An unsymmetric laminate does not bend just because B is not zero. With no applied force and no applied moment, this model predicts no deformation at all. B only links a load to a response: pull an unsymmetric panel in its plane and it also curls or twists, even though no moment is applied. A symmetric panel under the same pull stays flat: it stretches (and, if unbalanced, also shears in its plane) but does not curl or twist.

Flat-held and free stiffness differ for unsymmetric laminates

Flat-held and free stiffness differ for unsymmetric laminates

The two stiffness numbers for an unsymmetric laminate answer different questions. Flat-held (curvature-constrained) stiffness uses A alone and assumes something stops the panel from curving. Free stiffness lets it curve with zero applied moment and solves the full relation including B and D; it is never higher, and in most directions lower, because the panel can curl as well as stretch. For a symmetric laminate the two are identical.

Real unsymmetric panels can also warp as they cool after curing, because each ply shrinks differently in different directions. That temperature effect is not modeled here, and the curled panel in the interactive is not a picture of it: every curl drawn above is the response to the stated in-plane load.

Supporting detail: Addendum 46 — How the laminate stiffness and the free-panel response are calculated.

This is linear, small-deflection classical laminate theory with perfectly bonded plies. It does not predict strength, first-ply failure, delamination, buckling, temperature or moisture effects, or how a real panel behaves once its deflection is comparable to its thickness.

Supporting detail: Addendum 47 — Primary mechanics source and model boundary.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Bending and Laminating Wood

Compare steam bending, kerf bending, bent lamination and veneering by what changes shape and what holds the result.

Separate the bending step from the cutting and bonding steps

Separate the bending step from the cutting and bonding steps

Bending changes the shape of wood and belongs to Forming. A complete route can use several of the five process categories: cutting thin strips or kerfs is Separating; bonding layers is Fabricating. Veneering bonds a thin wood facing to a supporting base, so it is not automatically a bending operation.

Wood remains in the Wood & Composites material family. See Manufacturing Process Categories for the process model. Wood structure, moisture and engineered-wood products belong to the wood-as-a-material topic; here the question is how to obtain a shape.

What bends, and what retains the shape?
RouteWhat changesMain trade-off
Steam bendingOne piece is softened, bent over a form and restrained while it sets and dries.Continuous grain can follow the curve, but stock quality and bend severity strongly affect success.
Kerf bendingPartial-depth slots let the remaining thin web bend; slots close on the inside.Material removal reduces the intact section and leaves visible or concealed slots.
Bent laminationThin strips bend together over a form; cured adhesive holds the assembly.Repeated curves are practical, but strip preparation, glue lines and springback matter.
VeneeringA thin facing bonds to a substrate, flat or curved.The base supplies the shape and support; a face veneer alone is not a thick structural member.
Steam makes suitable wood more bendable; the form holds the curve

Steam makes suitable wood more bendable; the form holds the curve

Heat and moisture soften the wood's lignin-rich matrix, allowing the piece to deform more readily. The wood does not become a liquid. It is bent around a form, a shaped support, and held while it cools and dries. Clear, straight-grained white oak and ash are common candidates; species alone does not guarantee a successful bend.

The outside of a bend tends to stretch while the inside compresses. Too much stretching can split the outer fibers; too much compression can wrinkle the inner face. Grain deviations, drying history, moisture, thickness and bend radius all matter. A larger radius is a gentler bend. There is no single radius-to-thickness ratio that works for every piece.

Supporting detail: Addendum 48 — Why heat and moisture work together.

These are process concepts, not steaming-equipment instructions. Equipment use belongs with Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping.

Bent lamination uses thin strips and adhesive to retain a curve; Practice

Bent lamination uses thin strips and adhesive to retain a curve

Thin strips bend more easily than one solid piece of the same total thickness. Bent lamination brings prepared strips together with adhesive over a form, then restrains them until the bond has developed as specified for that adhesive. The strips commonly run with their grain along the curve. Alternating grain direction is not a requirement of bent lamination.

Springback is the tendency for a bend to open when restraint is removed. It can occur in both steam-bent and laminated parts. Thinner laminations can reduce springback for a given total thickness and curve, but adhesive behavior, layer count and material also matter. A trial bend establishes any form compensation; there is no universal correction percentage.

Do not rank every “hot/wet” part above every “cold/dry” part in strength. Compare the actual grain path, remaining section, bond quality, loading and service conditions.

Practice bending-route selection

Kerf bending trades an intact section for easier curvature

Kerf bending trades an intact section for easier curvature

A series of partial-depth slots on the inside of the intended curve leaves a thin continuous web on the outside. The slots narrow as the piece bends. Slot depth and spacing, the remaining web and the desired radius determine how it deforms.

This method can suit curved coverings where the slotted side is concealed. It also removes load-carrying material. Filling or bonding the slots does not automatically restore the properties of the original uncut board. A backing or supporting structure may be part of the design; structural performance needs its own justification.

Veneer follows a prepared substrate; it does not replace it

Veneer follows a prepared substrate; it does not replace it

Veneer is a thin wood layer. A substrate is the base it is bonded to. Veneering puts a chosen grain appearance over that base and can cover a flat surface or an appropriate curved form. The substrate must have the intended shape and a sound, even bonding surface.

In book matching, adjacent veneer leaves are opened like book pages to make a mirrored pattern. In slip matching, leaves are placed beside one another in the same orientation for a repeated pattern. Neither arrangement is the same as alternating structural grain directions through a panel's thickness.

Unequal face and back construction can encourage a panel to warp. Veneer thickness, grain, adhesive and the balancing back layer belong in the layup design. Glue selection and detailed bonding methods belong to wood fabrication; engineered panels belong to the material topic.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Buying Lumber and Board Feet

Separate sales size from measured size and calculate board footage using an explicit dimension convention.

Nominal size is a name; actual size is what fits; Practice

Nominal size is a name; actual size is what fits

A nominal lumber size identifies a product category. Dry, surfaced construction lumber sold as a 2 × 4 commonly measures 1-1/2 × 3-1/2 in in cross-section. Rough, green, specialty, and reclaimed stock can differ. Measure the piece when fit matters.

Drying and surfacing help explain the difference, but nominal names are not a universal subtraction rule. Do not assume that removing the same amount from every nominal size will give its actual dimensions.

Use Measurement Language for units and Dimensional Analysis for conversions. Keep length units explicit: an 8 ft board is 96 in long, not 8 in.

Practice: actual width

Quarter thickness and surfacing describe different things

Quarter thickness and surfacing describe different things

Hardwood thickness is often named in quarter-inch increments before final surfacing: 4/4 means nominal one-inch stock and 8/4 means nominal two-inch stock. Neither guarantees that much finished thickness. Drying, flattening, and planing reduce the usable material.

Rough
Sawn surfaces remain; allow material for flattening and sizing.
S2S
Surfaced on two sides, normally the two broad faces. Do not assume the edges are straight or ready for a joint.
S4S
Surfaced on all four long sides: both faces and both edges. Ends are not included in the four.

Ask for the supplied thickness, width, length, moisture condition, grade, and surfacing. A thickness label alone is not a complete purchase specification.

A board foot is volume, not length

A board foot is volume, not length

One board foot (BF) is the volume of a piece 1 in × 12 in × 12 in: 144 cubic inches. With thickness and width in inches and length in feet:

BF = thickness (in) × width (in) × length (ft) / 12.

If all three dimensions are in inches, divide by 144 instead. Multiply by the number of identical boards only after finding the volume of one.

Supporting detail: Addendum 49 — Why the mixed-unit formula divides by 12.

State the measuring convention. A physical-volume calculation uses actual dimensions. A sales tally may use nominal thickness or other trade rules and may round individual board measurements. Ask the seller; do not replace a quoted tally basis with finished dimensions without saying so. The examples here explicitly specify their basis and use unrounded arithmetic until the final answer.

Keep purchase tally and finished volume separate; Interactive; Practice

Keep purchase tally and finished volume separate

Suppose a seller specifies a tally using nominal 1 in thickness, measured 7 in width, and 9 ft length. The tally is 1 × 7 × 9 / 12 = 5.25 BF.

If that board finishes at 3/4 in thick with the same width and length, its physical volume is 0.75 × 7 × 9 / 12 = 3.9375 BF, or 3.94 BF to two decimals. These answers describe different quantities. The finished volume does not change the stated sales agreement.

A board tally is not a finished-parts yield. Allow for saw cuts, defects, flattening, trimming, and the layout of the parts. Appearance grades and structural grades answer different questions; an attractive board is not automatically suitable for a load-bearing member.

Build a list of boards below to compare the sales tally with actual volume, calculate cost, and estimate a material allowance.

Say which allowance you mean. This calculator treats the allowance as the share of the material you buy that will not end up in parts: BF to buy = needed BF ÷ (1 − allowance), so a 20% allowance means buying 1.25 times what you need. Many shop guides instead say “add 20%” to what you need (× 1.20), which is a different definition and buys less. Both are used; check which one a source or an instructor means before you compare numbers.

Practice: sales tally Practice: physical volume Practice: several boards Practice: all-inch dimensions Practice: material allowance
