Choosing a Woodworking Machine

Start with the required cut, surface or hole, then match the machine and cutter to that result.

Choose the required geometry before choosing the machine; Checklist

Choose the required geometry before choosing the machine

A machine name does not describe a finished part. First state the result: a straight edge, a curved outline, a flat face, a hole or a round profile. Then consider the workpiece dimensions, accuracy, surface quality and available tooling. The machines below remove material and belong to Separating.

This is a selection guide, not an operating procedure. Machine-specific use belongs with Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Equipment Operating Procedure. Grain and moisture are covered in the wood-as-a-material topic; the operation selected here depends on those properties.

  • Describe the surface or cut that must exist when the operation is complete.
  • Identify which existing face or edge can locate the workpiece.
  • Check machine capacity and whether the cutter can reach the feature.
  • Decide whether the cut is final size or leaves material for another operation.
Match the cut to a suitable starting machine; Practice

Match the cut to a suitable starting machine

Common choices; capacity and tooling can change the selection
Required resultStarting choiceWhat distinguishes it
Straight rip to widthTable sawThe fence locates a straight reference edge for a parallel cut.
Square crosscut or miterMiter saw; table saw with crosscut sled or miter gaugeA miter is an angled cut across the width. Crosscut capacity limits the workpiece size.
Dado across a faceRouter; table saw with compatible dado toolingA dado is a flat-bottomed channel across the grain. Not every table saw accepts a dado set.
Curved outside outlineBand saw or jig sawA band saw uses a continuous loop; a jig saw uses a short reciprocating blade.
Resaw into thinner boardsBand sawThe cut passes through the board's width to divide its thickness. Resaw capacity and blade selection matter.
Enclosed interior openingJig saw or scroll sawA starter hole gives blade access without a cut from the outside edge. A scroll saw suits fine, intricate work; its blade can be threaded through the hole.
Flat reference face; straight square edgeJointerEstablishes geometry before sizing. See Milling Rough Lumber Square.
Target thickness and parallel facesThickness planerUses an already flat reference face; it does not reliably flatten a warped board by itself.
Edge profile, rabbet or repeated outlineRouterBit shape makes the profile; a template guides repeated outlines. A rabbet is a recess open along an edge.
Round spindle or bowl-like formWood latheThe workpiece rotates around an axis while a cutting tool removes material.
Located hole with controlled angle and depthDrill pressA guided spindle and depth stop support repeatability; bit type determines the hole's form.

Read How Saws Cut Wood before choosing a saw blade. Table saws can crosscut as well as rip; jig saws and scroll saws are not band saws.

Practice resaw selection Practice interior cuts

Router bits make profiles and channels; templates repeat shapes; Practice

Router bits make profiles and channels; templates repeat shapes

A router spins a router bit. Straight or spiral bits make channels and pockets; roundover and chamfer bits change an edge's profile. A bearing-guided bit or guide bushing can follow a template, which is a pattern used to reproduce an outline.

Routers may be handheld, mounted in a table or moved by a CNC machine. A shaper commonly carries profile cutters on a table-mounted spindle. Both shape wood, but their cutters and mounting systems are not interchangeable merely because the resulting profile looks similar.

Supporting detail: Addendum 51 — Why “router bit” is more useful than “end mill” here.

Practice template selection

Spindle and faceplate turning put grain differently relative to the axis

Spindle and faceplate turning put grain differently relative to the axis

In typical spindle turning, grain runs mainly parallel to the rotation axis, as in a handle or table leg. In typical faceplate or bowl turning, grain runs mainly across the axis, as in a bowl blank. Faceplates and chucks are workholding methods; the name alone does not guarantee the grain orientation.

Turning removes material to make circular features. It does not bend the wood. Lathe Operations explains metal-lathe operations as a separate topic; wood turning has different tools and workholding practices.

Choose a drill bit for the hole's bottom, edge and diameter; Practice

Choose a drill bit for the hole's bottom, edge and diameter

Common wood-hole tools
BitUseful resultLimit to remember
TwistGeneral holes in a range of diametersThe usual point leaves a conical bottom in a blind hole.
Brad-pointAccurately located holes with clean entry edges in woodThe center point projects beyond the cutting lips.
ForstnerClean-sided blind recess with a largely flat bottomMost leave a small center-point mark; “flat” does not mean perfectly featureless.
SpadeEconomical larger holes where finish is less criticalUsually leaves a center-point recess and a rougher result.
Hole sawLarge through-hole by cutting around a coreLeaves a plug; it does not clear a flat-bottomed pocket.

A drill press improves control of axis and depth; it does not make every bit suitable for every hole. Cutter geometry, workpiece support and setup still affect accuracy.

Practice bit selection

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Drying and Conditioning Wood

Compare drying methods, prepare stock for its service environment and calculate moisture content on an oven-dry basis.

Condition the wood for the environment where it will be used

Condition the wood for the environment where it will be used

Conditioning changes material properties. Drying removes moisture so wood can be prepared for a particular use. It does not permanently freeze the moisture content: dried wood still exchanges moisture with surrounding air. Review the wood-as-a-material topic for the underlying grain and movement behavior.

Not every use requires dried wood, but closely fitted indoor furniture generally does. Choose a target moisture content appropriate to the expected indoor temperature and humidity, then check the actual stock before final machining and assembly. A mill's drying target and a suitable in-service range are not necessarily identical. “Kiln-dried” describes a process; it is not a measurement of what the board contains today.

For indoor furniture in most of the United States, the USDA Wood Handbook recommends 8% average moisture content, with individual pieces at 6–10%, at installation. Regional guidance differs: the dry Southwest uses a 6% average (4–9% for individual pieces), while damp, warm coastal areas use an 11% average (8–13%). Use these as starting points and match the actual service environment. See Table 13–2 and Figure 13–1, page 13–5.

Supporting detail: Addendum 52 — Why the indoor moisture target depends on the building.

Air drying follows the weather; kiln drying controls the conditions

Air drying follows the weather; kiln drying controls the conditions

Two drying routes, often used in sequence
RouteHow it worksWhat it can and cannot do
Air dryingBoards are stacked with spacers called stickers so air can reach their faces, with support and protection from direct rain.Needs little purchased drying energy, but speed and final moisture depend on climate, species and thickness. Outdoor air drying may not reach the target for heated indoor furniture.
Kiln dryingA chamber controls temperature, humidity and airflow through a drying schedule.Can reach lower, more controlled moisture levels. An unsuitable schedule can cause cracks, internal damage, distortion or residual stress.

Drying faster is not always drying better. The outside of a board may dry while the center remains wet. Suitable schedules manage this difference; elapsed time or a dry-feeling surface alone does not prove the board is ready.

Radio-frequency and microwave systems both use electromagnetic energy for dielectric heating, but the terms are not synonyms. Industrial systems control frequency, power and moisture removal; this is a process overview, not a household-microwave procedure.

Acclimate stock with airflow and repeated measurements; Checklist

Acclimate stock with airflow and repeated measurements

Acclimating means giving lumber time to approach the conditions in the intended working or service environment. There is no reliable fixed number of days for every board. Thickness, initial moisture, species and humidity all affect the time required.

  • Identify the intended service environment before choosing the moisture target.
  • Support boards flat with aligned stickers and space for airflow.
  • Check several boards and locations with a suitable moisture meter, using its species and temperature corrections where required.
  • Record repeat measurements and look for stability, not just one favorable reading.
  • Recheck after major material removal or a change of storage environment before final fitting.

Meter depth and measurement method matter: a surface reading can miss a wetter core. Keep stock in suitable conditions after drying. Joint design still needs to allow movement; see Wood Joinery and Fasteners.

Calculate moisture content using oven-dry mass as the denominator; Practice

Calculate moisture content using oven-dry mass as the denominator

On the oven-dry basis used for wood, MC (%) = (initial mass − oven-dry mass) / oven-dry mass × 100. Both masses must refer to the same sample and use the same units. “Initial” means the sample's mass before the moisture determination; it need not be freshly cut green wood.

For an illustrative sample with initial mass 230 g and oven-dry mass 200 g, the water removed is 230 − 200 = 30 g. Then MC = 30 / 200 × 100 = 15.0%.

Supporting detail: Addendum 53 — Why dividing by the initial mass answers a different question.

Practice moisture content Practice rounding moisture content

Distinguish temporary softening from permanent treatment

Distinguish temporary softening from permanent treatment

Heat and moisture in steaming can soften wood enough for bending. The softening is conditioning; changing the shape is Forming. The part must be restrained as it dries and sets, and some springback can occur. Species, grain quality, thickness and bend radius govern success; there is no universal bending radius for all wood.

Other treatments have specific purposes. Resin impregnation introduces resin into wood; impreg is resin-treated wood, while compreg also uses compression during manufacture. Increased dimensional stability or hardness can come with changes in other properties. Decorative color is not what defines compreg.

Pressure treatment is a delivery method, not a promise of every kind of resistance. Preservative treatment and fire-retardant treatment use different systems for different purposes. Neither the word “treated” nor “pressure-treated” alone establishes water exclusion, chemical resistance or suitability for an application. Use the treatment identification and product specification.

Wood–plastic composites made by combining wood particles or fibers with a polymer are a materials topic. Irradiation is not a universal requirement for making them. Finishing preparation is covered in Preparing and Finishing Wood; chemical handling belongs in Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Engineered Wood Products

Compare veneers, strands, particles, fibers, and laminations to choose a wood product for its intended use.

Engineered wood changes the arrangement of the wood

Engineered wood changes the arrangement of the wood

Engineered products combine wood pieces with binders to make sheets or members that a single log could not supply as consistently. They belong to Wood & Composites: the wood supplies much of the structure, while the binder holds the selected arrangement together.

Engineering redistributes natural variability; it does not make all products equally strong, waterproof, or free of manufacturing defects. Select the product grade, thickness, orientation, exposure suitability, and fastening details for the job.

Plywood cross-laminates veneers to restrain movement

Plywood cross-laminates veneers to restrain movement

A veneer is a thin sheet of wood. In plywood, adjacent veneer layers commonly have grain at right angles. Each layer restrains the cross-grain movement of neighboring layers, making the panel more stable in its plane than a comparable wide solid-wood board.

Conventional plywood commonly has an odd number of plies in a balanced layup, with matching face-grain directions. Odd ply count is not a universal rule for every panel construction. The grain direction of the faces still matters to panel stiffness and strength; cross-lamination does not mean equal performance in every direction.

Plywood serves cabinet boxes, furniture panels, sheathing, and subfloors when the appropriate product is selected. Face appearance, core voids, bond durability, and panel rating vary. A decorative face veneer does not establish a structural rating.

Choose the sheet by its structure and service conditions; Practice

Choose the sheet by its structure and service conditions

Sheet goods: useful differences
ProductStructure and strengthsLimits and typical uses
OSB: oriented strand boardWood strands bonded in layers with deliberate orientation. Structural grades provide useful panel strength and stiffness.Common in wall, roof, and floor sheathing. Follow the marked strength direction and rating. Edges can swell when wetted; it is not a decorative substitute for every plywood face.
MDF: medium-density fiberboardFine wood fibers and resin produce a smooth surface without solid wood's visible grain pattern. Well suited to painted profiles.Common in interior cabinet doors and trim. Heavy; ordinary grades swell with moisture. Edge fastening needs suitable hardware and preparation. Moisture-resistant grades are not automatically waterproof.
ParticleboardSmall wood particles bonded into an economical, comparatively uniform panel; useful as a substrate under a decorative surface.Common in interior furniture and laminate countertops. Ordinary grades are moisture-sensitive, edges are vulnerable, and fastener holding and shelf deflection need attention.

Painting a moisture-sensitive board does not turn it into a product rated for prolonged wet exposure. For wood dust and product-handling hazards, use Personal Protective Equipment and Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets rather than inferring precautions from a product's name.

Practice: painted panel Practice: rated sheathing Practice: laminate substrate

Glulam and LVL put wood along the member

Glulam and LVL put wood along the member

Glulam bonds lumber laminations with their grain generally parallel to the member's length. It is used for structural beams and columns, including large members and curved forms.

LVL (laminated veneer lumber) bonds thin veneers with grain predominantly along the member. It is part of the structural composite lumber group and is commonly used for beams and headers over openings. It is not simply thick plywood: its layup favors lengthwise performance.

Use the manufacturer's design information for a particular structural product. Product names alone do not give allowable loads, spans, or permission to cut holes. Lamination and bending methods belong to the later wood forming and fabricating topics.

Further reading on wood properties and products

Further reading on wood properties and products

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Gluing and Clamping Wood

Match the adhesive to the fit and exposure, then prepare the surfaces and hold the assembly through the specified cure.

Build the joint around sound, closely fitted glue surfaces

Build the joint around sound, closely fitted glue surfaces

Glue needs clean, sound surfaces and a joint designed for the load. For ordinary PVA wood glue, prepare mating surfaces that contact closely without being forced into shape. Paint, finish, dust and old adhesive can prevent a reliable bond.

Long grain is a surface running along the wood fibers; end grain exposes their cut ends. A long-grain edge joint can provide broad, continuous contact. End grain can absorb liquid adhesive rapidly and leave too little at the interface; a plain end-grain butt joint also has limited bonded area and unfavorable loading. End grain can bond, but adding more glue does not automatically make that joint equivalent to a fitted tenon or lap.

Supporting detail: Addendum 55 — What “stronger than the wood” actually demonstrates.

Choose the adhesive for fit, exposure and repair needs; Practice

Choose the adhesive for fit, exposure and repair needs

Adhesive families: starting points, not product specifications
AdhesiveUseful forFit and exposure limits
PVA, including yellow wood glueClosely fitted wood-to-wood joints in furniture and cabinetry.Not a structural gap filler. Water resistance varies from interior formulations to products rated for specified wet exposure; color does not establish the rating.
Polyurethane wood glueMoisture-curing bonds where the product lists the materials and exposure.Expanding foam is not sound replacement wood in a loose joint. Clamp to control expansion. Do not transfer one product's water rating to the whole family.
EpoxySome repairs, mixed-material joints and gaps using a suitable resin, hardener and structural filler.Mix the specified ratio. A fairing filler meant for easy sanding is not necessarily a structural adhesive filler. Water and temperature performance depend on the system and cure.
Hide glueTraditional furniture and repairs where future disassembly matters.Hot hide glue and liquid hide glue have different working times. Close fit is important; heat and moisture can weaken the bond as well as aid repair.
CA (cyanoacrylate)Small parts, small repairs and rapid positioning.Thin and gel grades suit different gaps. Short working time and often brittle bonds limit its use for large assemblies or impact loads; check the exact grade.
Construction adhesiveBuilding assemblies and dissimilar materials listed on the cartridge.A broad product category, not one chemistry. Bead size, gap limits, compatibility, support time and water resistance are product-specific. It is not automatically suitable for precision furniture joints.

Hot-melt adhesive sets quickly as it cools and is useful for temporary positioning or packaging. Do not assume that quick set gives a durable furniture bond.

Practice adhesive selection

Separate working time, clamp time and full cure

Separate working time, clamp time and full cure

Open time is the period after spreading adhesive during which the surfaces may remain apart. Assembly time includes getting the joint together and into clamps; manufacturers may define open and total assembly time separately. Clamp time is how long the assembly must be restrained. Full cure is when the adhesive reaches its specified cured properties under the stated conditions.

These are not interchangeable. A joint that can leave the clamps may still be unready for machining or service loads. Check the exact product's instructions for temperature, moisture, timing and exposure. A fixed “30 minutes for all yellow glue” rule is unreliable.

PVA requires time for water loss and bond development; one-part polyurethane depends on moisture; epoxy working time depends on its resin/hardener system and temperature. Hot hide glue has a short working window as it cools. CA can fix parts very quickly, so trial assembly is especially important. Construction adhesive often needs continued support after initial grab.

Supporting detail: Addendum 56 — Where to find product-specific instructions.

Use clamps to close the joint, not to repair a bad fit; Checklist

Use clamps to close the joint, not to repair a bad fit

Apply enough pressure to seat the surfaces and maintain alignment, following the adhesive instructions. Excess force can dent the wood, bow a panel or force out too much adhesive. A gap that closes only under severe force is a fitting problem.

Bar and pipe clamps span large assemblies; C-clamps apply local pressure; spring clamps suit light holding jobs. Cauls are straight blocks or beams used to distribute pressure and help keep faces aligned. Protect visible surfaces and prevent the cauls from becoming glued to the assembly.

A small, reasonably even bead of squeeze-out can indicate coverage, but it does not prove the entire bond is sound. A dry spot may be hidden inside. Excess glue can seal the surrounding pores and leave a pale patch under stain. Remove it by a method appropriate to the adhesive and surface; do not smear it into a wider area. Inspect again before finishing.

  • Dry-fit all parts and place the clamps and cauls within reach.
  • Read the product's assembly, clamp and cure requirements.
  • Spread adhesive as directed, assemble within its working time and close the joint.
  • Check alignment, flatness and diagonals where a rectangular assembly must be square.
  • Inspect squeeze-out and clean surrounding surfaces appropriately.
  • Keep the joint restrained and unloaded for the specified intervals.

Choose the geometry in Wood Joinery and Fasteners first; choose the surface treatment in Preparing and Finishing Wood after the assembly is ready.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Grain and Moisture Movement

Connect grain orientation and moisture changes to board movement, defects, and design choices.

Follow the grain through the face, edge, and end

Follow the grain through the face, edge, and end

Grain describes the direction of wood cells. Figure is the visible pattern created by growth structure and the way the wood is cut. A board's broad surface is its face, its narrow long surface is its edge, and its cut end exposes end grain. Face and edge grain usually run generally along the board; they are not separate botanical structures.

Wood is generally stronger in tension along the grain than across it. A short projection with grain running across its narrow base can split off even if the rest of the part is thick. Knots divert nearby grain, and sloping or interlocked grain makes a board less predictable.

During machining, a cutting edge can lift fibers ahead of the cut and tear them out. Grain direction helps predict that result, but does not replace the machine's operating procedure. See Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Equipment Operating Procedure for safety; wood separating and finishing are later topics.

Sawing orientation changes figure and movement

Sawing orientation changes figure and movement

Read the growth rings on the end of a board. Plain-sawn boards have rings more nearly parallel to the broad face and often show cathedral-shaped face figure. Quarter-sawn boards have rings more nearly perpendicular to the face; their width follows the radial direction more closely. Rift-sawn boards have an intermediate, oblique ring angle and commonly show straight face grain.

Quarter-sawn oak can expose conspicuous ray fleck. Rift-sawn oak is often selected for straight grain with less prominent fleck. Trade descriptions and angle boundaries vary, so inspect the end grain as well as the sales label. The diagram shows selected orientations, not a mill's complete cutting plan.

Moisture content uses oven-dry wood mass as its reference

Moisture content uses oven-dry wood mass as its reference

MC (%) = (wet mass − oven-dry mass) / oven-dry mass × 100. A sample weighing 150 g before drying and 100 g after oven drying has 50% MC. MC can exceed 100% because the reference is dry wood mass, not the original wet mass.

Water occupies cell cavities and is also held in cell walls. At the fiber saturation point, the walls are saturated while the cavities contain no free liquid water. Below this region, loss of water from the cell walls causes appreciable shrinkage. It is not one exact threshold for every species and condition.

Equilibrium moisture content (EMC) is the moisture content wood approaches in a particular surrounding humidity and temperature. A board can be dry today and absorb moisture later.

Green
Freshly cut or unseasoned; moisture varies greatly.
Air-dried
Dried by surrounding air; the achievable condition depends on the climate and storage.
Kiln-dried
Dried in a controlled chamber. This is a drying history, not a promise that the board will never move or that every kiln-dried product has the same MC.

Choose and acclimate material for its intended service environment. Use measurements to judge readiness; a fixed number of days cannot guarantee equilibrium for every thickness and starting condition.

Most movement is across the grain; Interactive

Most movement is across the grain

For normal straight-grained wood, shrinkage is usually greatest tangentially (along growth rings), smaller radially (across rings), and much smaller longitudinally (along the cells). Swelling reverses the moisture-loss trend. Actual amounts depend on species, grain orientation, and the moisture interval.

Do not apply a green-to-oven-dry shrinkage percentage directly to a small seasonal humidity change. A movement estimate needs a species-specific coefficient, board orientation, starting MC, and expected service MC. Reaction wood and juvenile wood can also depart from ordinary longitudinal behavior.

Estimate movement using starting dimension × coefficient × (final MC − starting MC), with both MC values within 6–14%. The attachment experiment below separates total width change from travel at a particular point.

Wood movement and attachment clearance — both moisture contents must be 6–14%.

Change = starting dimension × coefficient × (final MC − starting MC), with MC entered as a percentage (8, not 0.08). Negative means shrinkage; positive means swelling. Use the tangential coefficient CT for the width of a flat-sawn board or when the ring orientation is unknown, and the radial coefficient CR for the width of a quarter-sawn board or the thickness of a flat-sawn one.

Worked example: a flat-sawn white fir board 9.15 in wide at 8% MC, CT = 0.00245, reaching 11% MC: 9.15 × 0.00245 × (11 − 8) = 0.0672525 in wider, about 9.2173 in final width. The exact conversion starts at 232.41 mm and ends at about 234.118 mm. The Handbook's separately rounded 232 mm example ends at about 233.705 mm.

Predict: with one ideal fixed reference on a stationary support, does center fixing make the right edge move half as far, the same distance, or not at all, compared with fixing the left edge?

Same total width change, different edge travel: 8% to 11% MC
Fixed referenceLeft edge travelRight edge travel
Center0.0336 in outward0.0336 in outward
Left edge0 (fixed)0.0673 in outward

For uniform free strain, signed point displacement = (signed distance from the fixed reference ÷ installed width) × total width change. Center fixing halves the edge travel, not the total width change. A point closer to the reference travels less.

Compare available travel in each direction from the installed position. With 0.040 in outward travel, center-fixed edges remain inside the travel window, while the opposite edge of the left-edge-fixed board exceeds it. Drying reverses the movement: 8% to 6% MC gives 0.0224 in inward travel at each center-fixed edge, exceeding a separate 0.020 in inward allowance. Enough travel in one direction does not supply travel in the other.

Each estimate starts from the installed dimension and MC. Edge points are geometric tracking points, not a fastening layout. The support is stationary, with one ideal fixed reference and otherwise free uniform width change; friction, warp, strength, restraint stress and cracking are not calculated. Exceeding a travel window does not predict what the restrained board will do. A result within the window does not approve a joint.

Commercial lumber is rarely perfectly flat- or quarter-sawn, so this method can overestimate width shrinkage and underestimate thickness shrinkage. Board properties and ring angles vary. These are approximate estimates; no correction or safety factor is added. Outside 6–14% MC a different method applies.

Moisture-movement source: USDA Wood Handbook (2021), chapter 13, Equation 13-3 and Table 13-5. The point-travel equation is derived geometry under the stated assumptions.

Name the distortion before deciding what to do; Practice

Name the distortion before deciding what to do

Defects described by shape
DefectWhat you see
CupCurvature across the width: the face resembles a shallow trough.
BowCurvature along the length, out of the broad face's plane.
CrookCurvature along the length within the face's plane; the edge wanders sideways.
TwistThe corners no longer lie in a common plane.
Check / splitA separation along the grain. A check may be confined to a surface or end; a split extends through the piece.

Unequal shrinkage, uneven moisture, and irregular grain can contribute to warp. Drying stresses can open checks and splits. A stain is a color change, not automatically proof of lost strength; decay is a different concern.

Practice: cup Practice: bow Practice: crook Practice: twist Practice: check

Allow solid wood to change width; Checklist; Practice

Allow solid wood to change width

A solid-wood tabletop needs room to expand and contract across its grain. Suitable slotted attachments let it move relative to a supporting frame. A panel held in grooves needs clearance rather than rigid restraint across its full width. Details depend on the joint and expected movement.

Choose the fixed reference deliberately, then check travel from each attachment's installed position in both moisture directions. Slot length alone does not give clear travel: the fastener occupies space, and its starting position divides the available movement. The experiment above uses clear travel directly rather than inferring a hardware size.

Do not assume that a finish locks moisture out. It can slow moisture exchange, but does not eliminate seasonal movement. Plywood often solves a panel-stability problem better than simply making a solid board thicker.

  • Identify the grain direction and width that can move.
  • Check moisture against the intended service environment.
  • Inspect for warp, splits, and grain interruptions before laying out parts.
  • Check that attachments allow the expected movement.

Wood conditioning and fabricating cover drying and joint-making in more detail; Engineered Wood Products compares alternatives to solid lumber.

Practice: center-fixed travel Practice: directional clearance

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

How Saws Cut Wood

Match teeth to grain direction, leave room for chips, and include the saw's kerf in every cutting layout.

Teeth remove chips; the kerf is the wood they remove

Teeth remove chips; the kerf is the wood they remove

Sawing is a Separating process: each tooth removes a small chip, and successive teeth make a slot. The slot's width is the kerf. The space ahead of a tooth, called the gullet, carries chips out of the cut.

Many steel saw teeth have set: teeth bend slightly to alternating sides so the cut is wider than the blade body. Carbide-tipped circular blades commonly get that clearance from tips wider than the steel plate instead. Set and kerf are related, but they are not the same measurement.

This page explains cutting concepts. For operation, use Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Equipment Operating Procedure.

Rip along the grain; crosscut across the fibers

Rip along the grain; crosscut across the fibers

A rip cut runs along the grain, usually to reduce a board's width. A crosscut runs across the grain, usually to reduce its length. Describe the cut relative to the grain, not just as a long or short cut.

Ripping teeth commonly have a flat, chisel-like cutting edge. Crosscut teeth commonly have alternating bevels that score and sever fibers at the sides of the cut. These are useful patterns, not universal rules: combination and specialty blades use other arrangements.

Supporting detail: Addendum 58 — Why tooth geometry changes the surface.

Balance tooth count, chip space and hook angle

Balance tooth count, chip space and hook angle

For circular blades of the same diameter, more teeth generally share the work into smaller bites at the same feed and rotational speed. That can improve a crosscut surface, but leaves less space for chips. Thick ripping cuts often benefit from fewer teeth and larger gullets. “Thicker wood needs more teeth” is not a general rule.

Band and reciprocating blades commonly specify teeth per inch (TPI). Tooth spacing must suit the thickness engaged in the cut. A coarse blade has more chip space; a finer blade can suit thinner stock and finer work. Blade width also matters on a band saw: a narrower blade can follow a tighter curve.

Hook angle describes the tooth face's lean relative to a radial line on a circular blade. More positive hook generally gives a more aggressive bite; low or negative hook is less aggressive. Machine type and the blade maker's intended application matter along with the desired finish. A ripping blade is not automatically appropriate on a miter saw.

See Feeds and Speeds for the relationship between tooth engagement, feed and cutting speed; metal-cutting settings do not transfer directly to wood.

Supporting detail: Addendum 59 — Blade terminology reference.

Count cuts before calculating strip yield; Practice

Count cuts before calculating strip yield

Start with the usable width after any edge preparation. Let W be usable board width, s the required strip width and k the kerf, all in the same units. These ideal layouts assume straight cuts, exact dimensions and no extra finishing allowance.

One cut per strip, leaving an offcut: used width = n(s + k). The maximum whole number is floor(W / (s + k)); “floor” means round down. For a 12 in board, 3 in strips and a 1/8 in kerf, floor(12 / 3.125) = 3 strips. Three cuts use 9.375 in, leaving 2.625 in. Four strips alone use 12 in, leaving no room for the cuts.

All final pieces use both original outside edges: W = ns + (n − 1)k for an exact partition. There are only n − 1 cuts between n pieces. If a layout leaves an extra offcut to separate, count that extra cut too. Draw the layout before choosing a formula.

Real layouts also allow for defects, edge trimming and later machining. Kerf is material removed, not useful strip width.

Practice strip yield Practice cuts between pieces Practice the remaining width

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Milling Rough Lumber Square

Establish one flat face and one square edge before making the opposite surfaces parallel and cutting to length.

A jointer establishes flatness; a planer establishes thickness

A jointer establishes flatness; a planer establishes thickness

Stock is the material a part starts from. Rough lumber may have uneven surfaces or warp. A jointer removes material to establish a flat face. With that face as a reference against a square fence, it can establish a straight edge at 90° to the face.

A thickness planer cuts the upper face relative to the face supported by its bed. With a flat reference face down, it makes the opposite face parallel and brings the board to thickness. Jointing both faces separately does not ensure they are parallel.

Supporting detail: Addendum 60 — Why a planer alone can preserve a bow.

Build reference surfaces in order: face, edge, thickness, width, length; Practice

Build reference surfaces in order: face, edge, thickness, width, length

This is the geometry sequence for preparing rough stock. It assumes enough material remains for the finished dimensions and that the stock fits the equipment. It is not a machine setup guide; use Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping for operation.

  1. Face-joint: establish a flat face and mark it as the reference.
  2. Edge-joint: use the reference face to establish one straight edge square to it.
  3. Plane: place the reference face against the planer bed and bring the opposite face parallel to it at the required thickness.
  4. Rip: use the straight reference edge to locate the cut; make the opposite edge parallel at the required width.
  5. Crosscut: establish a square end, then cut the other end to the required length.

Any preliminary breakdown into shorter, oversized blanks comes before final sizing. Leave allowance for the later cuts; an early rough crosscut is not the final crosscut in this sequence.

Practice the milling order Practice the reference face

Try the order on a warped board: what each machine removes or copies; Interactive

Try the order on a warped board: what each machine removes or copies

Pick a board with cup, bow, twist or crook, as defined in Grain and Moisture Movement. Choose the next operation, predict the result, then check it with a straightedge, winding sticks and a square. Try the planer first, then the reference order, and compare. This is reference-surface geometry, not machine operation: see Jointer, Table Saw and Equipment Operating Procedure before using the machines.

Square a warped board. With JavaScript, this card is an interactive board you can machine one operation at a time: pick a cup, bow, twist or crook, predict what the jointer, planer or table saw will do, and check the result with a straightedge, winding sticks and a square. The figures below come from the same model.

The reference order on four warped boards

Each strip starts with a rough board (warp exaggerated to be visible) and applies face-joint, edge-joint, plane, rip and crosscut. Every later step uses a surface an earlier step made true.

Planer first: thickness becomes even, the cup stays

Worked example (cupped board). The rough board’s face A is 6.2 mm out of flat. In the flexible-board example the planer presses it flat, cuts the top parallel to the pressed underside, and releases it: thickness becomes 19.0 mm, but face A is still 6.2 mm out of flat and face B now copies the cup (6.1 mm). Flattening face A afterwards leaves the board 13.1–19.0 mm thick, short of 19 mm. In the reference order the same board finishes at 19.0 × 110.0 × 520.0 mm with every check at zero within the model’s tolerance.

Cup board: what each step leaves (model mm). Planer: flexible board pressed flat by the rollers.

Planer firstRough board6.26.136.06.9°
Planer: face A on the bed, plane to 19 mm6.26.119.06.9°
Jointer: flatten face A0.06.112.9–19.00.8°
Jointer: straighten edge A against the fence0.06.112.9–19.00.0°

Edge before face. On the twisted board, jointing edge A first and face A second leaves edge A 1.9° out of square: where the twisted face touched the fence, its local angle set the edge angle. Flatten the face first, then use it against the fence.

What the model assumes

  • Geometry only, in millimetres. The board is a grid of points on its faces, edges and ends. Every cut is a plane or a surface built from straight lines, and a point outside the cut slides inward along the board until it reaches the cut, so no step can add material.
  • Jointer face: an ideal long, flat table. The board rests on its lowest points; the cut stays parallel to that resting plane and passes continue until the deepest hollow is reached. The pass count shown is an illustrative step, not a depth-of-cut recommendation.
  • Jointer edge and table-saw rip: the edge rests on its outermost points along a long table or fence, so the cut is straight along the length. The face touching the fence or table beside the cutter sets the edge angle, so a flat face gives a square edge and a twisted face does not.
  • Planer, flexible-board example: feed-roller pressure is assumed to bend the board until its overall curve lies on the bed; the top is cut parallel to that pressed underside and the warp returns on release. A stiffer board, or one shimmed on a flat sled, can instead keep its resting attitude; switch the planer to the rigid case to compare. Neither case is a rule for every board or planer.
  • Crosscut: each end is cut perpendicular to face A and edge A near that end, first end just to clean up, second end at the finished length.
  • Warp amounts (cup 6 mm, bow 14 mm, twist 12 mm, crook 16 mm on a 640 × 150 × 36 mm blank) are deliberately large illustrative values, not measured boards. Machine setup, feed, guards, snipe, tearout, kickback and moisture movement are outside this model.
Check geometry instead of counting machine passes; Checklist

Check geometry instead of counting machine passes

One pass is not proof that a surface is ready. The result of each stage is the reference for the next. Flatness means a surface lies in a plane; parallel faces maintain a constant separation; square surfaces meet at 90°.

  • Check the reference face for flatness with a straightedge and for twist with winding sticks, a matched pair of sighting bars.
  • Check the reference edge for straightness and squareness to the face.
  • Measure thickness at several positions after planing.
  • Check width, parallel edges, end squareness and final length.
  • Recheck dimensions and geometry if material removal releases stresses and the board moves.

Stop and reconsider the intended dimensions if flattening would make the board too thin or too narrow. No sequence can recover material already removed. Use How Saws Cut Wood to account for kerf in the width and length layout.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Preparing and Finishing Wood

Prepare a uniform surface, distinguish color from protection and choose a finish for appearance, wear and repair.

Remove each grit's scratches before moving to a finer abrasive; Practice

Remove each grit's scratches before moving to a finer abrasive

Start with the least coarse abrasive that removes the actual defects efficiently. Higher grit numbers generally mean finer particles within the same grading system. A possible bare-wood sequence is 80 → 120 → 150 → 180, but sound, smooth stock may start later. Stop at the grit recommended for the chosen stain or finish; 220 is not a universal destination.

Each step removes the previous step's scratches. Jumping straight from a coarse grit to a very fine grit leaves deep scratches that the fine abrasive removes slowly. Inspect under light across the surface, remove dust between steps and replace clogged abrasive. Finish hand sanding along the grain where practical; machine sanding also requires control of pressure and motion.

Do not use prolonged sanding to hide a poorly fitted joint. It can round edges, dish a surface or sand through a thin veneer. Remove glue residue before coloring; a smooth glue patch may still reject stain.

Practice grit order

Treat raised fibers, defects and open pores as different problems

Treat raised fibers, defects and open pores as different problems

Water can raise loose fibers and make a previously smooth surface feel rough. When the finishing system calls for it, lightly dampen bare wood, let it dry, then sand the raised fibers lightly with the final preparation grit. This grain raising step reduces roughness under later water-based coats. Heavy sanding can expose fresh fibers and restart the problem.

Preparation products do different jobs
Product or stepPurposeCheck before using it
Defect filler or puttyFill a small hole or surface defect.Some products harden and sand; others remain softer and belong after finishing. Color and stain uptake may differ from wood. Sawdust mixed with glue does not reliably stain like the surrounding wood.
Grain/pore fillerFill open pores for a level surface, especially under a glossy film.Choose compatible filler and test whether it goes before or after coloring. Filling pores is optional when visible texture is wanted.
Pre-stain conditionerReduce uneven stain absorption on blotch-prone wood.It can lighten or alter the result; it does not guarantee uniform color. Follow the compatible stain system and its timing.
Sanding sealerProvide a readily sanded initial coating in a compatible system.It is not required under every finish. The wrong sealer can reduce adhesion or durability.

Bleaching changes wood color chemically; it is not the same as staining. Product chemistry determines the sequence, drying and any required follow-up preparation. Do not use a universal “bleach immediately after final sanding” rule. Consult Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets and Personal Protective Equipment for chemical handling and protection.

Use stain or dye for color, then decide what protection is needed

Use stain or dye for color, then decide what protection is needed

Pigment stain contains fine solid particles that lodge in pores and surface texture. It can emphasize grain and partly obscure it. Dye dissolves in its carrier and can give transparent color; it can still absorb unevenly. Some commercial stains contain both pigment and dye. A gel stain has a thicker consistency and often gives more surface color control on vertical or blotch-prone work.

Coloring alone is not normally the protective finish. Follow the product's application and wipe-off interval: leaving ordinary wiping stain on indefinitely is not a dependable way to make it darker. Test the complete stain-and-topcoat sequence because the clear coat changes the appearance too.

Compare a low-build oil finish with a protective surface film

Compare a low-build oil finish with a protective surface film

Choose by the service conditions and exact formulation
FinishAppearance and useTradeoff
Drying oils, such as linseed or tung oilUsually applied thinly for a low-build, grain-enhancing surface.Easy to renew in many applications, but thin oil treatments usually give less wear and spill protection than a suitable film. Drying oil cures; mineral oil does not cure the same way.
ShellacA resin coating available in different colors; useful for furniture and compatible sealing applications.Repairable, but vulnerable to alcohol and heat. Check wax content and compatibility before applying another finish over it.
LacquerA family of film coatings often used for furniture and sprayed production work.Many dry quickly; conventional solvent lacquers can be repaired by re-dissolving the surface. Catalyzed products cure differently and are not equally repairable.
Varnish/polyurethaneFilm-forming resin systems often selected for wear and spill resistance.Repair and recoating need preparation. Modern varnishes commonly use synthetic resins. Exterior protection requires an exterior formulation; “varnish” alone does not promise UV resistance.
Water-based clear coatingsOften chosen to retain a lighter color; may use acrylic, polyurethane or blends.Water-based identifies the carrier, not a separate guarantee of durability. Grain raising and intercoat adhesion need attention. Color change depends on both coating and wood.
Wax or paintWax offers a low-build, easily refreshed surface. Paint supplies opaque color in a film.Wax alone offers limited protection. Paint hides grain and needs compatible preparation, primer where specified, and a suitable topcoat system.

Names such as “Danish oil” or “tung oil finish” may describe blends rather than pure oil. Read the product description. No ordinary finish makes wood completely moisture-proof or eliminates the movement allowance in Wood Joinery and Fasteners.

Match application method and recoat timing to the product

Match application method and recoat timing to the product

Brushing suits many small assemblies; use a compatible brush and maintain a wet edge without repeatedly working a coating that has begun to set. Wiping gives thin, controllable applications when the product is designed for it. Spraying can coat complex shapes evenly but needs suitable equipment, setup and the safety controls in Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.

Roller coating suits suitable products on broad surfaces. Industrial curtain coating passes panels through a flowing sheet of finish; dip coating immerses parts. Electrostatic spraying requires a suitable coating and process setup to attract charged droplets to the work; ordinary dry wood does not automatically provide that setup.

Build the recommended coats and observe the recoat window. Sand between coats only as directed, with the specified abrasive and after sufficient drying. A fixed 320-grit rule does not fit every coating. Dry-to-touch is not full cure; allow the specified cure before service or final rubbing to adjust sheen.

Choose with a sample board and the expected wear in mind; Checklist; Practice

Choose with a sample board and the expected wear in mind

A frequently wiped surface needs a finish rated for that use; a lightly handled decorative object may favor appearance and easy renewal. Compare resistance to water, cleaning products, abrasion and heat, then consider color, sheen, repairability and available application equipment. A durable film is useful only if it adheres and cures properly.

  • Prepare a sample of the same wood with the intended sanding sequence.
  • Test any conditioner, filler and colorant together with the topcoat.
  • Record products, grits, application method and drying intervals.
  • Inspect color, texture and adhesion after the specified cure.
  • Choose the complete system before coating the finished assembly.

Supporting detail: Addendum 61 — Further product-specific preparation guidance.

Practice finish selection

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Wood Joinery and Fasteners

Choose joints and fasteners by the load, glue surfaces, assembly access and movement the connection must allow.

Choose the connection for the load and the grain direction

Choose the connection for the load and the grain direction

Joining separate parts is Fabricating. Start with the direction a load will push or pull, then choose the surfaces that carry it. A shelf needs support underneath; a frame must resist being pushed out of square. A joint that works well for one can be a poor choice for the other.

There is no single strongest joint. Wood species, dimensions, grain direction, fit, adhesive and loading all matter. A snug fit locates parts; it should not require enough force to split them. Most glued joinery is not an engineering interference fit.

Use the wood-as-a-material topic for grain and moisture movement. Use Gluing and Clamping Wood for bond preparation and Drying and Conditioning Wood before final fitting.

Recognize the shoulders, sockets and mating surfaces

Recognize the shoulders, sockets and mating surfaces

Simple joints: geometry, use and limits
JointWhat it is and where it fitsStrength consideration
ButtOne unshaped end or edge meets another piece. Common in simple assemblies.An end-to-face butt joint offers little resistance to opening without reinforcement. A long-grain edge-to-edge panel joint is a different, often effective glued connection.
RabbetA step cut along an edge or end receives another part; useful for cabinet backs and box corners.The shoulder locates the part and carries load in one direction. Glue or fasteners resist separation.
DadoA channel across the grain receives a shelf or divider.The bottom and shoulders provide bearing and location. Too deep a cut weakens the remaining side panel.
GrooveA channel along the grain; useful for a panel edge or drawer bottom.A groove can retain a panel while allowing it to move. Do not automatically glue a solid panel all around.
LapParts overlap. In a half-lap, material is removed from each so the assembled faces are flush.A fitted half-lap can give broad glue contact in frames; the cut also reduces each member's section.
MiterAngled ends meet, often two 45° cuts for a 90° frame corner.Hides end grain, but an unreinforced corner is vulnerable to opening. A spline, dowel or other reinforcement can help.
Add glue area, alignment or mechanical interlock where needed; Practice

Add glue area, alignment or mechanical interlock where needed

Reinforced and interlocking connections
JointGeometry and typical useWhat to check
Mortise and tenonA projecting tongue, the tenon, enters a matching socket, the mortise. Used in rails and legs.Long-grain cheeks provide glue area; shoulders help resist racking (being pushed out of square). Keep enough wood around the socket.
DowelA separate round wooden pin enters matching holes in both parts; used in furniture frames and alignment.Hole position, depth, dowel size and bonded embedment determine performance. A misaligned hole can prevent the shoulders from closing.
BiscuitA thin oval insert enters matching slots; useful for aligning panel edges during assembly.Do not assume an alignment biscuit gives the same reinforcement as a deep dowel or tenon.
Pocket screwA screw driven through an angled recess joins one part to another; common in face frames.Use the matching screw and jig setting. Clamp the parts against shifting; leave enough wood for the head and threads.
Box/fingerAlternating rectangular fingers mesh at a corner; common in boxes.Many glue surfaces resist separation when properly bonded. Straight fingers do not lock against withdrawal as dovetails do. Here “finger” means a box corner, not an industrial end-splice.
DovetailFlared tails fit between matching pins; common at drawer corners.The taper mechanically resists withdrawal in one direction. Thin pins, short grain or poor fit can still fail; orientation matters.

Practice choosing a shelf joint

Give screw threads something to grip and the head something to pull

Give screw threads something to grip and the head something to pull

A pilot hole guides the screw and reduces splitting in the receiving piece. A clearance hole lets the screw pass freely through the near piece so its head can pull that piece against the far one. A countersink is a tapered seat for a matching flat head. These holes do different jobs.

Choose pilot diameter from the screw maker's guidance for the wood and screw. A hole that is too small risks splitting; one that is too large removes thread engagement. Threads gripping both pieces before the gap closes can hold the pieces apart.

Use wood screws intended for the application. Drywall screws are intended to attach gypsum board; their head geometry and often brittle behavior make them a poor default for furniture or load-bearing wood joints. Purpose-designed structural screws also differ from ordinary wood screws. Match corrosion protection to the environment and any wood treatment.

Nails are quick to install and many tolerate bending better than hardened screws, but withdrawal resistance depends on shank form and grain direction. Brads are slender finish nails with small heads: useful for light trim and positioning, not a substitute for a designed load-carrying joint.

For repeated disassembly, consider bolts with nuts, cross-dowels, threaded inserts or cam connectors. These knock-down fittings use reusable mating hardware. Capacity still depends on the wood bearing around the fitting, edge distance and the specific hardware, not merely on having metal threads.

Let a wide solid-wood part move across its grain; Checklist; Practice

Let a wide solid-wood part move across its grain

A tabletop fastened rigidly across its width can split or distort as moisture changes. Use a connection designed to permit movement, such as tabletop clips or correctly oriented slotted screw holes. Locate the part while leaving travel in the direction it needs; a screw tightened so hard that nothing can slide defeats the slot.

A frame-and-panel assembly can hold a solid panel in grooves without gluing the panel's perimeter. A manufactured panel may need a different detail: do not assume every wood product moves like solid wood.

  • Identify the grain direction and the expected load in each part.
  • Dry-fit the joint and confirm that shoulders close without splitting or distortion.
  • Check fastener access, edge distance and the intended disassembly method.
  • Confirm that the attachment leaves room for cross-grain movement.

Practice allowing movement

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood

Wood Structure and Species

Read tree structure, distinguish botanical groups, and choose species for their properties rather than their names.

Wood belongs to the Wood & Composites family

Wood belongs to the Wood & Composites family

Wood is a cellular material whose properties depend on direction. Long cells run mainly along the trunk; their arrangement helps explain why a board carries loads and splits differently along and across its grain.

In the material-family model, wood belongs to Wood & Composites. Engineered wood products combine veneers, strands, particles, or fibers with binders. These products are why composites share this family. See Engineered Wood Products for the product choices; the material families and manufacturing process categories are foundation topics.

Supporting detail: Addendum 62 — What makes the cell walls work together?.

Read a trunk from bark to heartwood

Read a trunk from bark to heartwood

Bark
Outer bark protects the tree. Inner bark carries sugars made by the leaves.
Cambium
A thin growing layer produces new wood toward the inside and new inner bark toward the outside.
Sapwood
The outer wood conducts water and contains living storage cells. Many of its conducting cells are already dead at maturity.
Heartwood
Older inner wood no longer conducts water. Deposits can change its color and decay resistance; heartwood is not automatically stronger or decay-resistant in every species.
Pith and rays
The pith marks the central stem tissue. Rays run radially across the wood and contribute to storage and transport across the trunk.

A growth ring records a growth cycle. In many temperate trees, earlywood develops earlier in the season and latewood later. Their cells differ in size and wall thickness, creating visible bands. Ring contrast varies by species; ring width alone is not a strength grade.

Hardwood and softwood describe the tree, not its hardness; Practice

Hardwood and softwood describe the tree, not its hardness

Hardwoods come from angiosperm trees; softwoods come from gymnosperm trees, commonly conifers. Leaf shedding is not the defining test: some hardwood trees are evergreen, and some conifers shed their needles.

Balsa is a very soft hardwood. Southern yellow pine is a softwood but can be much harder than balsa. Ask about the species and the property you need, rather than treating the category name as a test result.

Supporting detail: Addendum 63 — How the cell structure differs.

Practice: balsa Practice: yellow pine

Match common species to the job

Match common species to the job

These are typical starting points, not grades or guaranteed design values. Inspect the actual board for grain, knots, moisture, and defects.

Common North American woods and familiar uses
Species or groupTypical characterCommon uses
PineVaries widely: eastern white pine is relatively light and soft; southern yellow pines are generally denser.Trim, construction lumber, furniture parts.
Yellow-poplar (tulip-poplar)Relatively soft hardwood; easy to machine and often painted. Not the same tree as aspen.Painted trim, cabinet parts, concealed furniture parts.
Red oakHard, prominent open pores and grain.Flooring, furniture, cabinetry.
White oakHard, prominent rays; heartwood is generally more decay-resistant than red oak heartwood.Furniture, flooring, cooperage such as barrels.
