Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals

Fasteners and Galvanic Corrosion

Choose mechanical joints for service access, thread compatibility and exposure to moisture and dissimilar metals.

Match the fastener to the assembly and its service access

Match the fastener to the assembly and its service access

Common mechanical joining components
ComponentPurposeDesign check
Bolt and nutProvide a removable threaded connection that can clamp parts together.Provide tool access, suitable thread engagement and a compatible strength and material specification.
WasherProvides a bearing surface or distributes load where the design requires it.A plain washer does not by itself prevent loosening or electrically isolate an entire joint.
RivetForms a retaining head through permanent deformation.Suitable for repeated sheet assembly; removal normally destroys the rivet. Blind rivets permit installation from one side.
Threaded insertProvides an internal thread in a host part.Select an insert designed for the host material and thickness. Check installation access, pull-out and resistance to rotation.

Standard fasteners often reduce dedicated tooling for short runs, but every fastener adds parts and assembly time. Riveting or automated fastening may suit long runs. Removability, inspection and repair can justify a threaded joint even when another method is faster.

A thread size alone does not specify a complete fastener; Practice

A thread size alone does not specify a complete fastener

The mating threads must agree in diameter, spacing and thread system. Similar-looking inch and metric parts are not interchangeable. Pitch describes axial spacing between adjacent thread forms; threads per inch describes a count over a unit length.

A purchase or drawing specification also needs the relevant length, head style, material or strength grade, coating and thread-fit requirements. The wrench size is not the thread diameter. Use the applicable thread reference and supplier drawing to decode a designation before choosing mating parts.

Read diameter and thread spacing separately
ExampleDiameterSpacing and system
1/4-20 UNCNominal thread diameter: 1/4 inch.20 threads per inch; UNC is the Unified coarse series. The pitch is 1/20 inch, not 20 inches.
M6 × 1Nominal metric thread diameter: 6 mm.Pitch: 1 mm between corresponding points on adjacent threads. The 1 is not a count of threads per inch.

These are thread-size examples, not complete fastener specifications. Nominal diameter identifies the size; tolerances govern the actual mating dimensions. A 1/4-20 thread and an M6 × 1 thread differ in both diameter and spacing.

Supporting detail: Addendum 65 — Sources for thread names and size examples.

Practice decoding a thread designation

For dimensional fit concepts, see Tolerances and Fits. For a permanently joined alternative, see Joining Metal.

Galvanic corrosion needs a metal pair, electrical contact and an electrolyte

Galvanic corrosion needs a metal pair, electrical contact and an electrolyte

Dissimilar metals can form a corrosion cell when they are electrically connected and share a conductive liquid, called an electrolyte. Moisture containing salts can provide that liquid. The more active member of the pair acts as the anode and may corrode faster; the other acts as the cathode.

A galvanic series ranks metals by their behavior in a specified environment. It helps screen combinations; it does not predict a service life. Alloy condition, surface films, wetting and exposed areas matter. A dry pair is not automatically a working galvanic cell.

Supporting detail: Addendum 66 — Why the wetted areas matter.

Supporting detail: Addendum 67 — Sources for galvanic contact, coatings and area effects.

Review the complete joint before calling a fastener compatible; Checklist; Practice

Review the complete joint before calling a fastener compatible

“Stainless” does not mean compatible with every metal, and a coating is not a permanent guarantee of isolation. Consider material pairing, durable electrical separation, drainage and a suitable protective finish together. An insulating washer under a head does not isolate a shank that still touches the hole wall.

  • Identify the base metal, fastener, washer and their coatings.
  • Identify where electrical contact and moisture can occur.
  • Check the material pairing for the actual service environment.
  • Review sleeves, washers or gaskets for complete isolation and mechanical suitability.
  • Provide drainage and an inspectable, maintainable finish.

Compatibility review does not replace structural sizing or joint design.

Practice spotting a corrosion risk

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals

Forming Metal

Compare casting, bulk deformation, sheet forming and powder metallurgy by shape, material, tooling and production quantity.

Choose the shape-making route before comparing production cost; Checklist

Choose the shape-making route before comparing production cost

Metal parts can begin as liquid poured into a mold, solid stock plastically deformed into a new shape, or powder pressed into a compact. Plastic deformation means a permanent shape change after the force is removed. Each route limits the shapes it can make and the tools it needs. A die is a tool that controls shape; a mold contains material while it takes shape.

These shape-making routes sit under Forming in the classification used by Manufacturing Process Categories. In metalworking references, forming often means solid-metal deformation specifically, with casting listed separately. Cutting is Separating; joining is Fabricating; property-changing treatment is Conditioning; surface protection or appearance is Finishing. Metals are one of the four families in Material Families, alongside Plastics, Wood & Composites, and Ceramics & Glass. Metal properties and heat treatment are separate topics.

  • Identify the alloy, overall shape, holes and thin regions.
  • State the quantity and whether the design will change.
  • Check tool access and how the part will leave the mold or die.
  • Compare tooling cost, repeatability and production rate.
  • Allow for trimming, machining, joining and finishing afterward.
Casting makes a shape by solidifying metal inside a mold

Casting makes a shape by solidifying metal inside a mold

Three casting routes and their trade-offs
RouteHow it worksTypical products and cost trade-off
Sand castingA pattern makes a cavity in bonded sand. Remove the pattern, assemble the mold, pour metal, then break away the mold after solidification.Pump housings and large machine bases. Relatively flexible tooling can suit small batches; making a new mold for every part adds work.
Investment castingA disposable pattern, often wax, receives a ceramic shell. Remove the pattern and fire the shell before pouring metal. Break away the shell afterward.Detailed brackets, valve parts and turbine components. Fine detail can reduce later machining, but pattern and shell preparation add time and cost.
Pressure die castingInject molten metal into a reusable metal die, let it solidify, then open the die and eject the part.Repeated aluminum or zinc housings. Expensive dies and equipment can pay off over long runs; alloy, size and geometry must suit the process.

There is no universal quantity at which die casting becomes cheapest. Obtain estimates for the actual geometry, alloy, tool life and required secondary operations.

Supporting detail: Addendum 68 — Sources for the casting routes.

A casting needs room to release, shrink and feed

A casting needs room to release, shrink and feed

The cope is the upper mold half; the drag is the lower half. The sprue leads downward from the pouring opening, and a runner and gate lead into the cavity. A riser supplies liquid metal as the casting solidifies and contracts. A core occupies space that must remain hollow.

Draft is a slight taper that helps a pattern or casting leave its tooling. A shrinkage allowance changes tooling dimensions to account for contraction. Neither is a universal number: alloy, geometry and process matter. Critical faces or holes may need machining afterward.

Supporting detail: Addendum 69 — Why a larger pattern does not replace a riser.

SFSA explains riser feeding and shrinkage voids.

Rolling squeezes, forging compresses and extrusion pushes through a die

Rolling squeezes, forging compresses and extrusion pushes through a die

Solid-metal forming routes
RouteShape and examplesTooling and quantity
RollingRotating rolls reduce thickness or produce a section. Sheet, plate and structural shapes are common products.Large equipment investment suits substantial throughput; a designer can often buy standard rolled stock.
Open-die forgingDies compress a solid workpiece without enclosing its whole outline. Examples include large shafts and rings.Relatively simple dies accommodate varied sizes; repeated positioning and later machining may be needed.
Closed-die forgingShaped die cavities guide metal flow into repeated parts such as connecting rods and wrenches.Dedicated tooling favors repeated production. Excess metal may form flash that is trimmed away.
ExtrusionA ram pushes a billet through a die opening. Long channels, rails and heat-sink profiles have a substantially constant cross-section.A dedicated profile die can serve many lengths. Cut ends, cross holes and local pockets require later operations.
Wire drawingPull wire through a reducing die to make it thinner and longer. This is different from pushing stock through an extrusion die.Die sets and handling equipment suit repeated lengths; several reductions may be needed.

Hot working occurs at temperatures and deformation rates that allow recrystallization, the formation of new grains, during deformation. Cold working occurs where that process does not remove the work hardening as deformation proceeds. The boundary depends on the metal and processing conditions; it is not one temperature for every alloy. Hot rolling permits large shape changes, while cold rolling commonly improves dimensional control and surface quality and can increase strength through work hardening.

Supporting detail: Addendum 70 — Cold forming does not guarantee an unchanged dimension.

Supporting detail: Addendum 71 — Sources for solid-metal deformation.

Sheet forming changes shape; blanking and shearing separate material; Practice

Sheet forming changes shape; blanking and shearing separate material

Bending changes the angle of sheet, as in a bracket or enclosure. A press brake uses a punch and die to make bends; adaptable tooling suits prototypes and short runs. Roll forming progressively bends strip through roll stations into a long profile, such as a channel. Its dedicated roll tooling favors repeated lengths. It is different from rolling sheet thinner.

Deep drawing pulls sheet from a flat blank into a die cavity to make a cup or shell. Tooling must control material flow to limit tearing and wrinkling. Dedicated tools suit repeat production. This is different from pulling wire through a reducing die.

Stamping names a press-based production route that can combine several operations. Bending and drawing are Forming; shearing and blanking are Separating. In blanking, the cut-out piece is the wanted blank; in punching a hole, the removed slug is usually scrap. A stamping line can therefore perform more than one process category.

Bend allowance accounts for the material length within a bend when developing a flat pattern. The sheet stretches on the outside and compresses on the inside. Use a validated bend table or supplier data for the alloy, thickness, radius and tooling; adding outside leg dimensions alone does not give the correct blank length.

Practice selecting a sheet process

Supporting detail: Addendum 72 — Sources for sheet forming and flat patterns.

Powder metallurgy presses particles, then bonds them by sintering

Powder metallurgy presses particles, then bonds them by sintering

In conventional press-and-sinter powder metallurgy, powder fills a die and is compressed into a green compact: a shaped part that is not yet fully bonded. Heating then bonds the particles during sintering, generally without melting the main metal throughout. Some systems include a liquid phase.

Small gears and porous bearings are typical products. Dedicated dies and presses favor repeat quantities and can produce a near-net shape, close to the finished dimensions. Tool access, ejection and density variation limit geometry; critical features may still require sizing or machining.

Supporting detail: Addendum 73 — Porosity can be useful or unwanted.

MPIF explains conventional compaction, sintering and secondary operations. This section describes that route, rather than every process that begins with metal powder.

Plan the separating operations that finish the geometry

Plan the separating operations that finish the geometry

Follow Milling Operations for machined faces and pockets, Lathe Operations for turned features, and Feeds and Speeds for cutting-data concepts. Use Tolerances and Fits to decide which dimensions require close control and Surface Texture and Finish to distinguish a surface requirement from a process name.

Forming is often only the beginning of a route. A casting can be machined, joined and coated. These pages compare processes for design; operating procedures belong in Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals

Heat Treating Metals

Choose a conditioning process by its goal: soften, refine structure, harden, improve toughness or reduce residual stress.

Heat treatment is conditioning: change structure to change properties

Heat treatment is conditioning: change structure to change properties

Heat treatment uses controlled heating, holding and cooling to change a metal's internal structure. It belongs to Conditioning in Manufacturing Process Categories. It can change properties without intentionally changing the overall shape, although distortion can occur.

The result depends on alloy, starting condition, section thickness and the complete cycle. Heating more or cooling faster is not automatically better. A treatment that strengthens one alloy can soften another.

Supporting detail: Addendum 74 — Steel microstructures are not the four steel families.

Anneal to soften; normalize suitable steels to refine structure

Anneal to soften; normalize suitable steels to refine structure

Annealing is a family of treatments used to soften material, restore ductility or adjust its structure. Full annealing of suitable steels includes slow cooling; annealing cold-worked metal can form new grains and restore formability. Not every anneal uses the same temperature or cycle.

Normalizing heats suitable steel into its austenitic range and then cools it in air. It can refine and make the structure more uniform after earlier processing. Air cooling and slow furnace cooling produce different results.

Choose the process for the desired condition. Do not apply one universal temperature offset to all steels.

Quench hardening usually needs tempering afterward; Practice

Quench hardening usually needs tempering afterward

Quench hardening heats suitable steel to form austenite, holds as required, then cools fast enough to obtain the intended hardened structure. It commonly raises hardness and strength but can reduce ductility and toughness. Cracking and distortion are possible.

Tempering reheats hardened steel below the temperature at which austenite begins to form. It adjusts the balance of hardness and toughness and reduces some quenching stresses. It is not simply heating “just below” one critical temperature; the required cycle depends on grade and target properties.

These concepts explain specifications; they are not operating instructions. Use the approved process for the identified material, equipment and quench medium.

Practice the purpose of tempering

Surface hardening puts wear resistance near the outside

Surface hardening puts wear resistance near the outside

A part may need a hard wear surface and a tougher interior. Carburizing adds carbon near the surface of suitable steel before hardening. Nitriding introduces nitrogen to develop a hard surface layer. These change surface chemistry.

Induction hardening heats a surface region electrically and then quenches it. It uses the steel's existing composition rather than adding carbon. It therefore needs a suitable starting steel. Case depth, surface hardness and core properties must be specified together.

Cold work strengthens; stress relief addresses locked-in stresses; Practice

Cold work strengthens; stress relief addresses locked-in stresses

Work hardening, also called strain hardening, occurs as metal is permanently deformed during cold working. It commonly raises strength and hardness while reducing remaining ductility. “Cold” here means below the relevant recrystallization range, not necessarily cold to the touch.

Stress relief reduces residual stresses left by processing. These are stresses that remain without an external load. The goal is often dimensional stability during later machining or service. Stress relief is not automatically a full softening anneal and does not guarantee zero distortion.

Practice restoring formability

Aluminum strengthening does not use steel's martensite route

Aluminum strengthening does not use steel's martensite route

Some aluminum alloys can be strengthened by solution treatment, quenching and aging. Solution treatment puts selected elements into solid solution; subsequent aging develops small particles that obstruct deformation. Aging can occur naturally or through controlled heating, depending on the alloy and required condition.

Solid-solution strengthening and precipitation strengthening are different mechanisms. Dissolved atoms provide the first; particles of another phase provide the second. Other aluminum alloys obtain much of their strength through cold work. Annealing can soften cold-worked material.

An aluminum temper describes its processing condition. It is not synonymous with the steel process called tempering. Preserve suffixes such as -O and -T6 when reading or writing a material description; consult the relevant alloy-temper specification for their exact meanings.

Supporting detail: Addendum 75 — Further reading on conditioning processes.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals

Joining Metal

Compare welding, brazing, soldering and mechanical assembly by joint access, heat input, production needs and service requirements.

Choose a joint around its load, access and need for disassembly

Choose a joint around its load, access and need for disassembly

Joining parts is Fabricating. First identify the metals, thicknesses, loading, service environment and whether the assembly must come apart. Then check access for the joining equipment and for inspection.

A welded frame can avoid a large casting tool, but fit-up, fixtures and inspection still cost money. A bolt-on cover allows service access, but needs clearance for the fasteners and tools. See Fasteners and Galvanic Corrosion for mechanical assembly.

This is a process-selection overview. For safety requirements, use Personal Protective Equipment, Fire Safety, Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets and Equipment Operating Procedure.

Welding joins the base metal; melting is not required in every process

Welding joins the base metal; melting is not required in every process

Fusion welding melts base metal at the joint, with or without added filler metal. The pool solidifies to form the joint. The common arc, oxy-fuel and resistance spot processes below are fusion processes.

Solid-state welding forms a bond without bulk melting of the base metals. Friction welding is one example. A solid-state process can still heat and alter nearby metal; “not melted” does not mean “unchanged.”

The heat-affected zone is nearby base metal whose structure or properties change because of the thermal cycle, without itself becoming weld metal. Selecting a process includes checking those changes and distortion, not merely whether a bead looks smooth.

Supporting detail: Addendum 76 — Sources for fusion welding, solid-state welding and the heat-affected zone.

Compare the heat source, filler and access of five welding processes; Practice

Compare the heat source, filler and access of five welding processes

Starting candidates for process selection
ProcessHow it works and where it fitsTrade-off
Oxy-fuel weldingA fuel-and-oxygen flame heats the joint; a separate filler rod may be added. Oxyacetylene can suit selected thin-steel work and repair.Flexible equipment, but slower and with more broadly distributed heating than many production arc processes.
SMAW / stickAn arc melts a flux-coated consumable rod. The coating supplies protection for the weld pool. Common for steel repair and construction work.Portable equipment and flexibility; rods need replacement and slag needs removal between appropriate stages.
GMAW (MIG/MAG)An arc melts continuously fed wire under external shielding gas. Common for repeated steel or aluminum fabrication with suitable wire, gas and settings.Continuous wire supports production and automation; shielding and equipment access must suit the job.
GTAW / TIGAn arc from a non-consumable tungsten electrode heats the joint under inert gas. Filler, when needed, is supplied separately. Useful for controlled joints in thin stainless steel and aluminum.Good control of heat and filler, but often slower than wire-fed production welding.
Resistance spot weldingOpposed electrodes press overlapping sheets together and pass current through them, forming a local fused nugget. Common in repeated sheet assemblies.Rapid repeat joints with suitable equipment and fixtures; conventional arrangements require access to both sides. Separate spots do not make a sealed seam.

Supporting detail: Addendum 77 — Why MIG is a familiar name but GMAW is the broader term.

Supporting detail: Addendum 78 — Sources for the five process mechanisms.

Practice choosing a joining method

Brazing and soldering melt filler while the base parts stay solid

Brazing and soldering melt filler while the base parts stay solid

In brazing and soldering, a molten filler wets the solid base parts. In a suitable close-fitting joint, capillary action draws filler into the gap. The usual dividing temperature is 450°C: the American Welding Society describes brazing fillers as having a liquidus above 450°C and soldering fillers below it. Liquidus is the temperature above which the filler is fully liquid. This distinction concerns the filler, not the flame temperature or the machine's setting. In both processes the base parts remain solid. Neither is simply a cooler version of fusion welding.

Brazing can join suitable dissimilar metals or attach a carbide tip to a steel tool body. Soldering is common in electrical connections. Choose filler and joint design for compatibility, temperature and loads; a soldered electrical connection is not automatically suitable for a structural load.

Joint clearance, surface condition and heating method matter. Brazing can be manual or performed in production equipment such as a furnace. Mechanization changes throughput and tooling costs; the process name alone does not identify the cheapest route.

Supporting detail: Addendum 79 — Sources for the filler-temperature distinction and capillary joint.

Specify the required joint, not just the name of the machine; Checklist

Specify the required joint, not just the name of the machine

  • Identify both base materials, thicknesses and any coatings.
  • Describe the joint location, overlap or preparation and equipment access.
  • State load, leak-tightness and appearance requirements.
  • Allow for distortion, inspection and any later machining.
  • Coordinate the finish and any assembly sequence constraints.

A drawing and its referenced specification communicate the required weld and acceptance criteria. A process abbreviation alone does not specify weld size, extent or quality. Likewise, a visually neat joint does not establish internal soundness. Heat-treatment selection is a separate topic.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals

Metal Stock Forms and Purchasing

Recognize stock shapes, distinguish size conventions, and specify enough information to receive the metal a design requires.

Stock is the material shape you buy before making the part

Stock is the material shape you buy before making the part

Stock is material supplied in a usable starting form. Choose a shape that leaves enough material for the finished part and any cutting or machining allowance. Buying the smallest possible shape can fail if saw cuts, surface cleanup or distortion consume the allowance.

Sheet, plate, bar and structural shapes use different size descriptions

Sheet, plate, bar and structural shapes use different size descriptions

What to specify for common forms
FormDescriptionSize information
Sheet and plateFlat products; plate is the thicker category under the applicable product convention.Thickness, width and length. There is no single sheet/plate boundary for every metal and specification.
BarSolid round, flat, square or hexagonal cross-section.Diameter, width and thickness, square side, or hex size across flats, plus length.
Structural shapesAngle, channel and I-shaped sections place material where the structure needs it.Section designation and dimensions, thicknesses and length under the relevant product system.

A gauge number is a sizing convention, not a universal thickness. Specify actual thickness and units when ambiguity would affect the part. Check the applicable material's gauge table if a drawing uses gauge.

Tube dimensions and nominal pipe sizes are not interchangeable

Tube dimensions and nominal pipe sizes are not interchangeable

Tube is commonly ordered by outside dimensions and wall thickness: outside diameter for round tube, or outside width and height for rectangular tube. State the length too.

Pipe commonly uses a nominal pipe size and a wall schedule. A nominal size is a label; it need not equal the measured outside or inside diameter. Use the applicable pipe dimensions table before calculating a fit or flow area. Structural tubing is not automatically suitable for pressure service.

Measure the right boundary. For round hollow stock, inside diameter equals outside diameter minus twice the wall thickness. The wall occurs on both sides of the opening.

Hot-rolled and cold-finished describe processing, not alloy identity

Hot-rolled and cold-finished describe processing, not alloy identity

Hot-rolled steel is shaped at high temperature and commonly arrives with mill scale and comparatively broad dimensional tolerances. Cold rolling or other cold-finishing operations can improve surface finish and dimensional control. Cold-finished bar may be drawn rather than rolled.

Cold work can increase strength and leave residual stresses. Removing material can release those stresses and move the part. Cold-finished does not automatically mean precision ground, and neither term guarantees a particular tolerance without a product specification.

Supporting detail: Addendum 80 — Why an attractive surface can still be the wrong purchase.

A purchase description must preserve alloy, condition, form and size; Checklist

A purchase description must preserve alloy, condition, form and size

An illustrative request is: 6061-T6 aluminum round bar, 25 mm nominal diameter × 500 mm cut length, quantity 2. Before purchasing, add the governing product specification, diameter and cut-length tolerances, finish and certification requirements that the design needs. This example is not a complete engineering specification.

  • Identify the alloy and required delivery condition from the design.
  • State the stock form and every necessary dimension with units.
  • Allow for saw kerf (material lost in the cut), cleanup and final machining.
  • State tolerances, quantity and any required material certificate.
  • Compare availability, cut charges, shipping and minimum orders as well as material price.
  • Confirm that the delivered label and documents match the order before using the stock.

Drops or remnants are leftover pieces that may reduce cost. Their identification and usable dimensions still need checking.

Estimate mass from cross-sectional area, length and density; Practice

Estimate mass from cross-sectional area, length and density

For uniform stock, mass = cross-sectional area × length × density. For a solid round bar, area = πd²/4. For round tube, area = π(D² − d²)/4, where D is outside diameter and d is inside diameter. Subtract the opening before multiplying by length.

Use the density for the actual alloy from a material data sheet and keep units consistent. A result in kilograms is mass; weight as a force also requires gravitational acceleration. See Geometry, Mass, and Force and Dimensional Analysis.

Practice bar mass with a supplied density Practice tube volume

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals

Metals and Their Properties

How bonding, grains and alloy condition affect the properties used to choose a metal.

Metal selection starts with the job the part must do

Metal selection starts with the job the part must do

A metal can carry a load, conduct current, transfer heat or resist wear. Those are different jobs. Start with the required behavior, then compare a particular alloy in a particular condition. An alloy combines a base metal with other elements to change its behavior.

Metals belong to the material-family foundations topic. Use Material Properties for the general property vocabulary; this page applies it to metals. Continue with Types of Steel, Nonferrous Metals, Metal Stock Forms and Purchasing and Heat Treating Metals.

Metallic bonding helps explain conduction and forming

Metallic bonding helps explain conduction and forming

In a metal, some electrons are shared throughout the structure rather than tied to one bond between two atoms. Their mobility helps metals conduct electricity and heat. Metallic bonding can remain intact while atoms rearrange during permanent deformation, which helps explain why many metals can be rolled or drawn.

Most engineering metals contain many tiny crystals called grains. Atoms have an ordered arrangement inside each grain; adjacent grains have different orientations. Grain size, alloy chemistry and processing history all influence properties.

Supporting detail: Addendum 81 — Why two pieces of the same alloy can behave differently.

Strength, hardness, ductility and toughness answer different questions

Strength, hardness, ductility and toughness answer different questions

Mechanical properties used when comparing metals
PropertyQuestion it answersSelection example
StrengthHow much stress can the material withstand? Yield strength concerns the start of permanent deformation; tensile strength concerns the maximum stress in a tensile test.A loaded bracket must resist permanent bending.
HardnessHow strongly does the surface resist local indentation?A wear surface may need hardness, but hardness alone does not predict every kind of wear.
DuctilityHow much permanent deformation can occur before fracture?A formed part needs enough ductility to survive bending.
ToughnessHow much energy can the material absorb before fracture?A part struck repeatedly needs resistance to fracture, not simply a hard surface.

Strong does not mean stiff. Stiffness describes elastic deflection. Hardening a steel can raise its strength substantially without a comparable change in its elastic stiffness. Geometry also affects how far a part bends.

Pull a tensile specimen: strength, stiffness, ductility and toughness on one curve; Interactive

Pull a tensile specimen: strength, stiffness, ductility and toughness on one curve

A tension test pulls a specimen of known size until it breaks and records force against stretch. Dividing by the original area and gauge length turns that record into an engineering stress–strain curve, and one curve answers four different questions: how stiff, how strong, how far it stretches and how much energy it absorbs.

The curves below are synthetic teaching curves, shaped to resemble common behaviour. Read the method from them, not the numbers for any real alloy.

Tensile test: one curve, four different properties. This fallback shows the same synthetic curves and calculations as the live lab.

A round specimen with a chosen gauge length L0 = 50 mm and diameter 12.5 mm (original area A0 = 122.7 mm²) is pulled by a moving crosshead. Engineering stress σ = F/A0 (N/mm² = MPa). Engineering strain ε = ΔL/L0 (mm/mm, shown here in %). Both use the original dimensions, so engineering stress falls after the neck forms even though the force is concentrated on a shrinking section.

  • Stiffness: the elastic slope, Young’s modulus E = σ/ε = 200 MPa ÷ 0.001 = 200 000 MPa = 200 GPa.
  • Yield strength (0.2% offset): draw a line with slope E starting at 0.2% strain; where it meets the curve, σy ≈ 250 MPa (at 0.325% strain). Specimen A then stretches along a level yield plateau (stress constant at 250 MPa up to 1.5% strain) before strain hardening makes the curve rise again.
  • Ultimate tensile strength (UTS): the highest engineering stress, 400 MPa at 20% strain. A neck begins to form after this peak.
  • Ductility: elongation after fracture ≈ εf − σf/E = 30% − 0.16% = 29.84%.
  • Toughness (tensile): the area under the curve to fracture, ∫σ dε ≈ 107 MJ/m³ (1 MPa × 1 = 1 MJ/m³ = 1 J/cm³) of work per original volume. For this gauge volume that is about 659 J. This is not fracture toughness KIC, which is measured on a cracked specimen.

Worked example: unloading leaves permanent set. Stop at ε = 10.0%, where σ = 371 MPa. Removing the load follows a straight line parallel to the elastic slope, so the elastic part σ/E = 371/200 000 = 0.185% springs back. Permanent set = 10.0% − 0.185% = 9.815%, or 4.91 mm on the 50 mm gauge length. Below the yield point the same rule gives zero set: at 0.1% strain and 200 MPa, 0.1% − 200/200 000 = 0.

Compare the four synthetic specimens. Each ranks differently on each property: the stiffest is not always the strongest, and the most ductile is not the toughest.

Read from the four synthetic curves (illustrative; not material data)
SpecimenStiffness E (GPa)0.2% offset yield (MPa)UTS (MPa)Elongation after fracture (%)Area to fracture (MJ/m³)
A: Ductile, low-carbon-steel-like20025040029.8107
B: Aluminium-alloy-like7026631012.638
C: Brittle, gray-iron-like100none: fractures first2150.10.42
D: Polymer-like (cold drawing)2.536.748.053.221

Specimen C fractures before the 0.2% offset line reaches its curve, so it has no offset yield strength in this test: the value is undefined, not zero. Specimen D (polymer-like) reaches its peak stress early and then draws a neck along the specimen; its offset value is shown only for comparison.

Model, assumptions and sources

The four curves are synthetic: piecewise cubic curves through chosen points, shaped to resemble common behaviour. They are not measurements, grades, certification values or design allowables. Real results depend on composition, processing, specimen geometry, test speed and temperature, none of which are modelled.

Unloading and reloading follow a straight line with the initial elastic slope E (an ideal elastic approximation, no hysteresis). The load never goes below zero: once the unload line reaches zero load the specimen is slack. Permanent set = ε − σ/E, never negative. Elongation after fracture uses the same rule at the fracture point.

The specimen length is drawn to scale. Its thinning before the peak keeps volume constant; the neck and the fracture are drawn only to show where deformation concentrates, not calculated from a necking or fracture law. True stress, strain rate, temperature and hardness are outside this lab.

The area under the curve is work per original volume in this tension test (MPa = MJ/m³). Impact and fracture-toughness tests measure related but different behaviour.

Sources: ASTM E8/E8M, Standard Test Methods for Tension Testing of Metallic Materials (the test method and its definitions; consult the current edition). W. D. Callister Jr. and D. G. Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction, chapter “Mechanical Properties of Metals” (engineering stress and strain, modulus, 0.2% offset yield, tensile strength and necking, ductility, toughness as area under the curve, elastic recovery on unloading).

Density, conductivity and corrosion can decide the choice

Density, conductivity and corrosion can decide the choice

Density is mass per volume. Compare equal volumes when comparing densities; a large aluminum part can still weigh more than a small steel part. Use Geometry, Mass, and Force and Dimensional Analysis for mass, weight and unit calculations.

Conductivity describes how readily heat or current travels through a material. Metals vary widely: choosing a good conductor is different from choosing a high-strength alloy.

Corrosion resistance depends on the metal and its surroundings. Stainless steel and aluminum can corrode. Water, salts, trapped moisture and contact with other metals can change performance. A protective surface film helps only while the environment allows it to remain effective.

Supporting detail: Addendum 82 — Why connecting two different metals can change corrosion.

Ferrous means iron-based; a magnet does not identify the grade; Practice

Ferrous means iron-based; a magnet does not identify the grade

Ferrous metals have iron as their base: steels and cast irons belong here. Nonferrous metals have another base, such as aluminum, copper or titanium. Nonferrous does not mean that no trace of iron can be present.

Magnetic response is a clue, not a material certificate. Some stainless steels are weakly magnetic or effectively nonmagnetic in certain conditions. Appearance and a magnet cannot establish an alloy, its temper or its strength.

Practice choosing a property

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals

Nonferrous Metals

Aluminum, copper alloys, titanium, zinc and magnesium as choices for weight, conductivity, corrosion and manufacturing needs.

Choose the useful property, then check the tradeoff

Choose the useful property, then check the tradeoff

Nonferrous metals have a base other than iron. They are not all lightweight, corrosion-proof or easy to machine. A useful first comparison names both the benefit and the constraint.

Starting points for material selection, not design allowables
MetalWhy choose it?Typical use and tradeoff
AluminumLow density, useful corrosion resistance and ready availability in extruded shapes.Frames and housings. Lower elastic stiffness than steel; alloy and temper strongly affect strength.
CopperHigh electrical and thermal conductivity.Conductors and heat-transfer parts. Relatively high density and cost; alloying usually reduces conductivity.
TitaniumUseful strength relative to weight and corrosion resistance.Aerospace and chemical-service parts. Material and processing costs can outweigh the weight saving.
ZincUseful casting behavior and ability to protect steel as a coating.Die-cast hardware and galvanized products. Temperature and load requirements limit use.
MagnesiumVery low density among structural metals.Light housings. Corrosion protection and suitable manufacturing procedures matter.

These are material-selection comparisons. For cutting operations, continue to Milling Operations, Lathe Operations and Feeds and Speeds.

Aluminum needs both an alloy label and a condition

Aluminum needs both an alloy label and a condition

Aluminum is sold in many alloys and conditions. Wrought products are shaped by processes such as rolling or extrusion. Their familiar four-digit labels are organized into series, including 1xxx through 7xxx. A series is a family, not a hardness scale: a higher first digit does not guarantee a harder or better part.

6061 and 7075 are common alloy labels to look for in supplier literature. Compare data for the actual product form and temper rather than treating either number as a complete specification. Cast aluminum uses a different designation system; do not transfer wrought-number rules to cast products.

A suffix such as -O or -T6 identifies a condition as part of an alloy-temper designation. It must stay attached to the alloy on an order. See Heat Treating Metals for why processing history matters.

The Aluminum Extruders Council defines the two tempers:

  • -O: “Annealed” — “Thermally treated to obtain the lowest strength temper.”
  • -T6: “Solution heat-treated and artificially aged.”

Use the governing product specification for an actual purchase.

Aluminum series 1xxx–7xxx identify purity or the main alloying additions

Aluminum series 1xxx–7xxx identify purity or the main alloying additions

Wrought aluminum series
SeriesPrincipal alloying element or purity
1xxxCommercially pure aluminum: at least 99% aluminum.
2xxxCopper.
3xxxManganese.
4xxxSilicon.
5xxxMagnesium.
6xxxMagnesium and silicon.
7xxxZinc.

Supporting detail: Addendum 83 — Source for the series table.

6061 favors fabrication; 7075 offers higher strength in the T6 condition

6061 favors fabrication; 7075 offers higher strength in the T6 condition

Compare like conditions: 7075-T6 has higher tensile strength than 6061-T6. The alloy number alone does not establish the strength of the material in hand.

6061 and 7075 at selection level
AlloyTypical usesFabrication considerations
6061Truck and marine frames; tanks.Weldable and readily machined. Welding can change the temper in the weld area.
7075Aircraft components, molds and industrial tooling.Good machinability, but generally considered unsuitable for welding because of cracking susceptibility.

Supporting detail: Addendum 84 — Sources and comparison limits.

Brass and bronze trade some of copper's conductivity for other properties; Practice

Brass and bronze trade some of copper's conductivity for other properties

Brass is principally a copper-zinc alloy. Depending on grade, it can offer useful forming or machining behavior for fittings, hardware and decorative parts. Do not assume every brass has the same machinability or suitability for contact with drinking water.

Bronze traditionally means copper-tin alloy, but commercial names also include aluminum bronze and silicon bronze. Bronzes serve in bearings, bushings, gears and corrosion-resistant hardware, depending on grade. The word “bronze” alone is not enough to buy a bearing material.

For a conductor, begin with conductivity requirements. For a bearing, begin with load, speed, lubrication and wear. The same copper-based family will not automatically win both comparisons.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals

Types of Steel

Carbon, alloy, stainless and tool steels, plus the difference between a steel family and a complete material specification.

Steel is iron-based, with carbon and other elements controlling behavior

Steel is iron-based, with carbon and other elements controlling behavior

Steel contains iron and carbon, often with additional alloying elements. Both composition and processing matter. The same grade can arrive softened for machining or hardened for service.

Use four practical groups: carbon steel, alloy steel, stainless steel and tool steel. These are useful buying categories, not four mutually exclusive chemical definitions: stainless and tool steels also contain alloying elements.

Carbon steel spans easy forming through hardenable cutting edges

Carbon steel spans easy forming through hardenable cutting edges

Relative carbon levels; actual grade limits come from the specification
GroupTypical behaviorTypical uses
Low carbonGenerally readily formed and welded; limited response to ordinary through-hardening.Sheet parts, brackets and general fabrication.
Medium carbonMore potential for heat-treated strength; forming and welding require more consideration.Shafts, axles and machinery parts.
High carbonCan develop high hardness after suitable treatment; less forgiving of forming and impact.Springs and some cutting tools.

These are trends, not a strength ranking of every item on a shelf. Compare the delivery condition and required properties before substituting one grade for another.

Alloy, stainless and tool steels solve different service problems

Alloy, stainless and tool steels solve different service problems

Choose a family, then qualify a specific grade
FamilyComposition idea and purposeUses and limits
Alloy steelIntentional additions such as chromium, nickel or molybdenum adjust properties and heat-treatment response.Loaded shafts and gears. Alloy steel is not automatically corrosion resistant.
Stainless steelChromium supports a protective surface film; other elements adjust performance.Food equipment, fittings and exposed hardware. Grade, cleaning and environment still matter.
Tool steelCarbon and alloy additions support hardness, wear resistance or performance at elevated temperature.Dies, punches and cutting tools. Heat treatment must balance wear resistance against chipping.

Use Heat Treating Metals to distinguish hardening from tempering. Hardenability means the ability to harden to depth under given cooling conditions; it is not the same as a measured surface hardness.

Grade labels identify a material; they are not a heat-treatment recipe

Grade labels identify a material; they are not a heat-treatment recipe

Common labels include 1018 and 1045 for carbon steels, 4140 for alloy steel, 304 and 316 for stainless steels, and O1, A2 and D2 for tool steels. Different designation systems have different rules. Do not apply a four-digit carbon-steel decoding rule to stainless or tool-steel labels.

On an order, identify the governing material specification, grade, delivery condition, form and dimensions. A short grade name alone does not specify strength, hardness, surface finish or dimensional tolerance. Ask for the required certification when traceability matters.

Use the current governing specification or the producer's grade sheet for composition limits and treatment requirements.

Decode carbon and alloy steel numbers; read stainless and tool grades separately

Decode carbon and alloy steel numbers; read stainless and tool grades separately

In the common AISI/SAE four-digit carbon and alloy steel system, the first two digits identify the steel series: 10 is plain carbon steel and 41 is chromium-molybdenum steel. The last two digits give nominal carbon content in hundredths of a percent.

Reading the series and nominal carbon content
GradeSeriesNominal carbon
101810: plain carbon18 → 0.18%
104510: plain carbon45 → 0.45%
414041: chromium-molybdenum40 → 0.40%

304 and 316 stainless: their chemistries are similar, but 316 has an added alloying element, molybdenum. This improves resistance to chloride exposure and urban or industrial pollution compared with 304.

Tool-steel groups: O1 is an oil-hardening grade, A2 is an air-hardening grade, and D2 is a high-carbon, high-chromium grade. These labels describe different tool-steel groups; they are not carbon-percentage codes.

Supporting detail: Addendum 85 — Sources and quoted designation meanings.

Cast iron is a separate iron-based material, and it can be machined

Cast iron is a separate iron-based material, and it can be machined

Cast irons generally contain more carbon than steels. Their properties depend strongly on how carbon appears in the structure. Gray iron contains graphite flakes and is useful for machine bases and housings where vibration damping matters; it is relatively brittle in tension. Ductile iron contains graphite nodules and can provide much greater ductility.

Casting creates the initial shape. Machining can then finish bores, faces and other accurate features. “Cast” and “machined” are not competing material identities. White cast iron contains substantial hard carbide and behaves differently from graphite-containing irons.

Watch the steel-family series at its original publisher; Practice

Watch the steel-family series at its original publisher

Metal Supermarkets hosts the five-part series: overview, carbon steel, alloy steel, stainless steel and tool steel. These are external learning resources, not specifications for purchasing or heat treatment.

Practice reading a material description

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Manufacturing Documentation

Bills of Materials

List the parts in an assembly and estimate each part's material share without confusing stock purchases with per-part consumption.

A bill of materials says what goes into one assembly

A bill of materials says what goes into one assembly

A bill of materials (BOM) lists the parts needed for a product. Give each part a stable number, a clear name, a quantity per assembly, a material and a make-or-buy designation. Identify the stock for made parts and the purchasing description for bought parts.

Made means the part needs a drawing and a route such as an operation method sheet. Bought means it arrives as a component; it still needs a size and specification so the buyer can obtain the correct item. Match the BOM revision to the assembly drawing. State whether quantities are per assembly or for the whole batch.

Material cost per part is its allocated stock share times stock price

Material cost per part is its allocated stock share times stock price

Estimated material cost per part = stock share allocated to that part × price of that stock unit. Keep both amounts on the same basis: length for constant-section bar, area for sheet of the same thickness, or mass when purchased by mass.

Allow for the saw cut's width (kerf), trimming and unusable stock. Finished-part volume alone can understate what making the part consumes. State how you allocate waste and reusable leftovers so two estimates can be compared.

Supporting detail: Addendum 86 — Consumption, purchase cost and batch yield answer different questions.

Worked BOM: one display label assembly costs $1.20 in allocated materials

Worked BOM: one display label assembly costs $1.20 in allocated materials

This original example matches DL-01 in Operation Method Sheets and Critical Dimensions for the Shop. All prices are invented teaching values, not quotations. Assembly DL-A, revision A, contains one made plywood plate and two purchased closed cord loops.

The 110 × 50 × 6 mm starting blank is allocated a 120 × 60 mm area of a 1200 × 120 × 6 mm birch plywood strip costing $18. The larger allocation includes room for cutting and trimming. Allocation share = (120 × 60) / (1200 × 120) = 0.05. Plate material estimate = 0.05 × $18 = $0.90.

DL-A revision A — quantities and material estimate per assembly
Part number / nameMake / buy; material and stockQuantityCost eachExtended cost
DL-01 / display label plateMake; birch plywood, blank 110 × 50 × 6 mm; allocated stock area 120 × 60 mm as above.1$0.90$0.90
DL-02 / closed cord loopBuy; waxed cotton cord, 1 mm diameter, 100 mm closed-loop circumference; example pack of 20 for $3.2$0.15$0.30
Total allocated material and purchased-component cost per assembly$1.20

Extended cost is quantity × cost each. The $1.20 excludes labor, machine time, tooling, consumables, taxes and delivery. It is not a complete manufacturing cost or a selling price. Broader cost roll-up and design-for-manufacturing decisions belong with manufacturing economics.

Buying one strip and one pack costs $21, even for one assembly. Unused material remains inventory; do not confuse that purchase total with $1.20 of allocated consumption.

Check quantities, units and waste before totaling the BOM; Checklist; Practice

Check quantities, units and waste before totaling the BOM

  • Match every drawing part number to a BOM row.
  • State the quantity per assembly and multiply once for the batch quantity.
  • Specify stock dimensions and material for made parts, and purchasing details for bought parts.
  • Use the same units in the stock-share numerator and denominator.
  • Document the cutting allowance and treatment of leftovers.
  • Multiply each quantity by its unit cost and sum the extended costs.

Keep unrounded intermediate calculations; round money to cents at the stated reporting step.

Practice stock-share cost Practice a BOM total

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Manufacturing Documentation

Critical Dimensions for the Shop

Choose dimensions from fit, function and interfaces, then give the maker and inspector the same references and limits.

A critical dimension controls fit, function or an interface

A critical dimension controls fit, function or an interface

A critical dimension is one whose variation can stop the part doing its job. Start with what touches another part, what must move or clear, and what locates the part. A hole's diameter may control whether a pin enters; its position may control whether two parts line up.

Critical does not mean “make every tolerance tight.” A tolerance is the permitted variation in a dimension. Choose it from the function, then check that the process and inspection method can achieve it. See Tolerances and Fits for limits and fits, Measurement Language for units and measurement language, and Surface Texture and Finish for surface requirements.

Give hole locations from named reference edges

Give hole locations from named reference edges

The original DL-01 display plate below illustrates a shop drawing. Its two suspension holes must stay at the intended locations; length and width mainly establish the display area. These are invented teaching limits, not a general specification for plywood or hanging hardware.

DL-01 revision A — drawing requirements
FeatureRequirementReason / inspection
Material and outlineBirch plywood; length 100 ±1; width 40 ±1; thickness 6 ±0.5 mm.Display area and thickness. Measure with calipers; check adjacent edges with a try square for no visible gap.
C — two through holesEach diameter 4.5 ±0.2 mm.Openings for the loops; use suitable plug gauges for 4.3–4.7 mm limits.
C — center positionsFrom L: x = 15 ±0.5 and 85 ±0.5 mm. From B: y = 20 ±0.5 mm for each.Consistent suspension locations. Check each coordinate from the stated edge.
Surface and edgesNo coating; no loose fibers, splits or separated plywood layers.Visual inspection after sanding; retain the dimensional limits.

All features have requirements, including those not marked C. See Operation Method Sheets for the manufacturing sequence and Bills of Materials for the matching parts list.

Worked record: correct horizontal separation, wrong locations

For this classroom comparison with DL-01 revision A, treat the following readings as exact mm values. The near-edge readings run horizontally right from L and vertically up from B to the nearest edge of each hole. Calculate each center using that hole's measured diameter.

  • Left hole: diameter 4.6; near edges 13.3 from L and 17.2 from B. Center x = 13.3 + 4.6/2 = 15.6 mm; y = 17.2 + 4.6/2 = 19.5 mm.
  • Right hole: diameter 4.4; near edges 83.4 from L and 18.3 from B. Center x = 83.4 + 4.4/2 = 85.6 mm; y = 18.3 + 4.4/2 = 20.5 mm.

Record the comparisons: both diameters meet 4.3–4.7 mm. Left x = 15.6 exceeds 15.5; right x = 85.6 exceeds 85.5, so both x locations fail. Both y locations meet 19.5–20.5 mm, including its endpoints. The horizontal separation is 85.6 − 15.6 = 70.0 mm, the nominal x-coordinate difference, but the pair is shifted right. These hole readings do not meet the drawing's separate location limits; correct horizontal separation alone does not locate the pair. This record compares only the stated hole readings, not the outline, thickness or surface requirements.

Supporting detail: Addendum 87 — How to check a center when a caliper touches the hole edge.

Dimension the part so it can be made without measuring the picture; Checklist; Practice

Dimension the part so it can be made without measuring the picture

Include the part identity, revision, material, units, overall dimensions, feature sizes and locations, thickness, and required finish. Supply enough views to remove ambiguity. Call a hole “through” when it passes through the material; otherwise specify depth.

Locate related features from a common reference where that matches their function. Do not give multiple independent dimensions for the same feature unless their relationship is clear. A redundant dimension can contradict the dimensions used to make the part.

  • Identify every mating surface, clearance and locating feature.
  • Choose references the maker can establish and the inspector can reach.
  • Check that each feature has a size, location and acceptance limit.
  • Remove conflicting or missing dimensions; do not rely on drawing scale.
  • Match the drawing revision to the method sheet and BOM.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Manufacturing Documentation

Making Silicone Molds from a Printed Pattern

Plan a one-part mold, document the product-specific mixing and curing conditions, and inspect a repeatable batch of castings.

A printed pattern defines the cavity in the silicone mold; Interactive; Practice

A printed pattern defines the cavity in the silicone mold

A pattern is the original shape copied by a mold. For a simple one-part, open-face mold, use a shape with a flat back and features that can be withdrawn through the opening. An original example is a small decorative relief tile with a flat back, gently sloping sides and no hooked details.

For a small batch of resin replicas, this is a casting task: liquid resin fills the mold cavity and cures. A fiber-reinforced shell made by wet hand layup builds layers of reinforcing fabric or mat with resin against a mold. Compare these routes in Plastic Forming Processes, then use Choosing a Plastic Forming Process to weigh material, geometry, quantity and tooling. Try the detailed-replica and reinforced-shell practice choices.

Draft is a slight taper that helps a part leave the mold. Let the shape widen toward the opening. A flat parting face, where the pattern meets the mold-box base, defines the open back of this mold. Avoid undercuts that hook behind the silicone; flexibility does not make every trapped shape removable.

A wide mouth does not rule out an interior hook. This illustrative model uses an exact-fit, centered, symmetric rigid 2D pattern and rigid cavity. Opening depth is 0; positive depth points down into the mold. The only permitted motion is outward translation upward at fixed orientation, into unobstructed space. Units are arbitrary consistent diagram units.

Exact piecewise-linear sections: stations are (depth, half-width)
ProfileStationsTrial pull 5Whole path
Taper(0,30), (40,20)1.25 side separationNo positive interference
Parallel(0,25), (40,25)Side contactNo positive interference; contact persists
Reverse taper(0,20), (40,30)1.25 interference per sideBlocked
Local shoulder(0,30), (20,22), (25,26), (40,15)Maximum 4 interference per side at depth 20Blocked despite widest mouth

At cavity depth d, an outward pull t places pattern half-width w(d+t) against cavity half-width w(d). Positive Δ(d) = w(d+t) − w(d) means overlap. For the local shoulder at t = 5, the positive interval is (50/3, 520/23), approximately (16.6667, 22.6087); endpoints are zero-contact boundaries.

The continuous path requires width to be nonincreasing with depth. A deeper section wider than a shallower section provides an obstruction. For each pose, Δ is linear between original and translated knots; checking these knots and solving zero crossings is analytical, not an animation-frame test. At t = 0 every profile is in initial contact. At t = 40 there is no interior overlap, but the reverse taper and local shoulder still have blocked paths: a clear endpoint does not prove a reachable endpoint.

Comparisons use a numerical threshold of 64 × machine epsilon × maximum half-width, separate from physical clearance and manufacturing tolerance. Values within that floating-point threshold are treated as contact. This is geometric interference only: it omits friction, adhesion, shrinkage, forces, damage, cure, rotation, lateral motion, deformation and unshown 3D features. No-interference does not establish practical release; a rigid obstruction does not establish flexible-silicone failure.

Remove unwanted layer ridges and support marks without losing important dimensions. Choose pattern preparation, any sealer and any release agent for the specific print, silicone and casting material. Follow the manufacturers' compatibility instructions and test a small prepared sample before committing the full mold.

Read the technical data sheet before choosing a mix or cure schedule; Checklist

Read the technical data sheet before choosing a mix or cure schedule

The technical data sheet (TDS) supplies processing instructions. The safety data sheet (SDS) supplies handling information; use Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets for that guidance. Neither a generic lesson nor a familiar-looking container replaces the instructions for the actual product.

  • Record the silicone product, batch identification and technical-sheet revision.
  • Record the A:B ratio and whether it is by mass (weight) or by volume.
  • Record working time, mixing procedure, bubble-removal requirements and cure conditions.
  • Check compatibility with the printed pattern, coatings, release agent and intended casting material.
  • Complete a small compatibility trial and inspect its cure before the full pour.

Working time is the available time to mix and place the material under stated conditions. It is not the demolding time. Cure instructions may distinguish demolding from full properties or further treatment. Record the actual temperature and times; do not substitute a universal overnight wait.

Supporting detail: Addendum 88 — Where to find product-specific instructions.

A ratio by weight is not automatically a ratio by volume; Interactive; Practice

A ratio by weight is not automatically a ratio by volume

Read what the given mass represents. These invented A/B examples teach arithmetic for two-component materials; they are not silicone or resin recipes. For A:B = a:b by mass and target total material mass M, mA = M a/(a+b) and mB = M b/(a+b). If A is already measured, mB = mA b/a.

Same 10:1 mass specification, different meaning of 220 g
GivenABMaterial total
220 g target total200 g20 g220 g
220 g of A alone220 g22 g242 g

Density connects mass and each component’s own volume: VA = mA/ρA and VB = mB/ρB. For a:b by volume, divide target total mass using weights aρA:bρB. For given A mass, VA = mA/ρA, VB = VA b/a, then mB = VBρB.

Use illustrative densities ρA = 1.2 g/mL and ρB = 0.8 g/mL with a 300 g target total:

Changing the basis while keeping 2:1 changes the specification
A:B specificationA mass / volumeB mass / volume
2:1 by mass200 g / 500/3 mL (≈166.6667 mL)100 g / 125 mL
2:1 by volume225 g / 187.5 mL75 g / 93.75 mL

The first row has a 4:3 component-volume ratio; the second has a 3:1 mass ratio. Those are equivalent descriptions of their respective batches. Converting 300 g to 0.3 kg keeps the same physical batch. Switching 2:1 from mass to volume does not. Individual component volumes do not establish mixed/cured volume, yield or cavity fill.

Ideal cumulative scale example: for 200 g A + 20 g B in a 35 g container, readings with no tare are 35 g empty → 235 g after A → 255 g after B. Tare once with the empty container on the scale and the readings are 0 g → 200 g → 220 g. The final reading includes A and B; B alone is 20 g. Container mass changes the gross reading, not the material ratio. This comparison does not re-tare after A.

Weigh with a scale suitable for the actual quantities and follow the product’s specified ratio basis, measurement and mixing procedure. The arithmetic assumes no material loss; it predicts no cure, exotherm, working time, compatibility or actual mixed/cured volume. The actual product’s TDS/SDS remain authoritative.

Practice a total-mass mix Practice a given-A mix

Document pattern preparation, pouring and cure as separate operations

Document pattern preparation, pouring and cure as separate operations

  1. Prepare the pattern and box. Inspect the print, complete the qualified surface treatment, secure its flat back to the box base, and check that the box contains the liquid. Set wall and backing thickness from the mold material and geometry requirements.
  2. Measure and mix. Record actual A and B quantities, the ratio basis and the start time. Follow the product's mixing instructions, including its directions for reaching material at the container walls and bottom.
  3. Reduce trapped air. Follow the product's bubble-removal and pouring instructions. A controlled pour into a low point can let the material rise around the pattern instead of repeatedly trapping air over its details. Vacuum degassing is product- and equipment-dependent; do not assume every silicone requires it or has enough working time for it.
  4. Cure and remove the pattern. Record temperature, elapsed time and the specified demolding condition. Inspect the mold surface and details after removal before using the cavity.
  5. Make a first casting. Follow the casting material's own mixing, release and cure instructions. Its ratio and timing need not match the silicone's. Inspect the first piece before repeating the batch.

Use Operation Method Sheets to give each operation equipment, settings, timing and a pass/fail check. Record what actually happened, including a changed pour method or a delayed demold, rather than copying the planned values into the result column.

Inspect each casting for voids, dimensions and consistency

Inspect each casting for voids, dimensions and consistency

A void is an unintended empty region. Inspect visible faces, edges and small details for pits, missing material and incomplete filling. A good exterior does not prove that the interior has no voids; choose further inspection according to the part's function.

Define batch checks before casting
CheckWhat to document
Shape and dimensionsDrawing limits, measurement method and actual readings for critical features.
Visible surfaceWhich faces matter and what counts as a reject. For a teaching relief tile, an example criterion is no visible pits or missing raised detail on the display face.
Cure and releaseProduct-specific acceptance condition; any tacky region, tearing or distortion observed on removal.
Batch consistencyCasting number, material batch, measured charge, mixing and cure times, appearance, dimensions, rejects and rework.

If a defect repeats at the same position, inspect the corresponding mold feature. If it varies between pours, compare the recorded process conditions. These are starting points for investigation, not proof of a cause. Change one factor, make a trial, and retain the results before revising the approved method.

Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Manufacturing Documentation

Operation Method Sheets

Turn a drawing into an ordered plan with equipment, setup, process settings and a check that proves each operation is complete.

A method sheet tells another person how to make and check the part

A method sheet tells another person how to make and check the part

A drawing describes the required part. An operation method sheet describes how to make it. A process plan or routing sheet serves the same planning purpose, although the amount of detail varies. Write one row for each operation, in the order it will be performed.

Start with the part number and name, drawing revision, date, material and raw stock size: the starting piece before machining or cutting. Use actual dimensions and units. A material family alone is not a purchasing specification; identify the material needed for this part.

What belongs in each operation row
FieldWhat the next person needs
OperationAn action and its intended result, such as drill two through holes.
Equipment and setup/toolingThe equipment, cutting tool, support, holding method and reference face or edge.
Process parametersSettings with units, or an identified approved setup instruction. Do not write an unexplained number for speed or feed.
Setup and cycle timeTime to prepare the operation, separate from time to repeat it on one part.
Pass/fail criteria and inspection toolsThe required result, permitted limits and how to measure or compare it.

Keep quality checkpoints, failed-part decisions, actual times and improvement notes with the sheet. Equipment permission and operating procedures still come from Equipment Operating Procedure; a method sheet is not machine training.

Establish reference surfaces before locating features

Establish reference surfaces before locating features

Choose the order around what each later step needs. Make a straight, square reference edge before measuring hole locations from it. Make features while there is enough material to support and hold the work. Inspect a feature before the next step hides it.

Holes may be easier to make before small parts are cut free from a larger piece. Final finishing usually follows cutting and drilling, so those operations do not damage the finished surface. Inspect afterward too: finishing can change dimensions.

Supporting detail: Addendum 89 — Why there is no universal operation order.

Worked method sheet: a hanging display label

Worked method sheet: a hanging display label

Original teaching example, not a production release. Part DL-01, display label plate, revision A. Material: birch plywood, starting blank 110 × 50 × 6 mm. Finished dimensions and acceptance limits are on the example drawing. Two purchased cord loops complete the assembly in Bills of Materials. No coating is specified.

This hand-tool route uses a supported blank, a fine-tooth handsaw, a drill press and sanding blocks. An actual shop must qualify its tooling and record machine settings before releasing the plan. The times below are invented planning estimates, not measured performance.

For three assemblies, the serial estimate is 10 + (3 × 13) = 49 minutes, assuming each setup is done once and all operations run one after another. Record waiting, interruptions and repeated setups separately when comparing with actual elapsed time.

Replace “make it right” with an action and an acceptance test; Checklist; Practice

Replace “make it right” with an action and an acceptance test

“Drill the holes neatly” leaves the next person guessing. “Drill two through holes at the drawing coordinates; check diameter and location against revision A” gives an action and a result, but still needs the equipment, support, tooling and settings in the row.

Pass means every stated criterion is met. Fail means identify and hold the part for a decision; do not quietly send it to the next operation. Rework is a specified additional operation that can bring the part into conformance. Removing more material cannot restore an undersize outside dimension or shrink an oversize hole.

  • Match the part, drawing and method-sheet revisions.
  • Check that every operation names equipment, tooling, holding and references.
  • Fill required settings with units before releasing the plan.
  • Give every quality checkpoint a measurable limit or an explicit comparison and an inspection method.
  • Define who decides rework or rejection when a check fails.

Practice operation order Find an incomplete step

Record what changed so the next batch can repeat the improvement

Record what changed so the next batch can repeat the improvement

Record setup time once per setup and cycle time per piece. State when each timer starts and stops; include inspection consistently. Keep quantity attempted, quantity accepted, scrap count and rework count. A reworked part may later pass, so these counts are not all separate groups to add together.

For each trial, record material identity, tool, setting and units, holding arrangement, actual measurements and the problem observed. A useful photo shows the reference edge, stop or tool position; caption it with the operation and revision. Use photos you have permission to share, with no personal information.

Example improvement record — a proposed trial, not a claimed result
ObservationChange to testEvidence to keep
Hole locations vary between pieces.Use the same reference edges and a verified locating stop instead of re-marking from different edges.Record each hole location before and after the change, batch size, setup time and rejects. Keep the acceptance limits unchanged.

Change one factor at a time where practical. Verify the first piece after a setup change before repeating it through a batch. If the change helps, update the method-sheet revision and keep the evidence. A faster operation that produces more rejects is not automatically an improvement.
