Addendum

Additional evidence, standards context, and background referenced from the main text.

  1. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Additive Manufacturing Process Families

    Addendum 1. Vocabulary, brand attribution and source scope

    ISO/ASTM 52900:2021 is the current fundamentals-and-vocabulary standard and describes additive shaping as successive addition of material. Its public abstract does not reproduce the full family list. The family structure and readable mechanisms here are checked against the NIST AM technology overview and the seven-family discussion in ORNL's Additive Manufacturing Design Guidelines. Stratasys's legal terms identify FDM as a registered trademark and PolyJet as a trademark; its PolyJet technology page documents the bounded photopolymer-droplet, UV-cure and support example used here. This page paraphrases sources and uses original graphics rather than copied standard or vendor art.

    Back to reference 1

  2. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Design for Manufacturing

    Addendum 2. Why the loosest tolerance is not automatically cheapest

    A tolerance that permits poor fit can increase assembly trouble, rework and failure. The goal is a manufacturable design that still meets requirements.

    Back to reference 2

  3. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Manufacturing Cost and Volume

    Addendum 3. Why a shorter cycle does not reduce every cost equally

    A 10% reduction in a time-based processing charge reduces that portion by 10%. Material, setup and rent do not automatically fall. Capacity limits, tool replacement, scrap and quantity discounts can change the model outside its assumed range.

    Back to reference 3

  4. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Manufacturing Cost and Volume

    Addendum 4. When there is no positive crossing

    Equal variable costs mean the lower fixed cost wins, or both routes tie everywhere if fixed costs also match. A negative crossing lies outside positive production quantities. For a fractional crossing, compare costs at the neighboring whole-part quantities. This is process-cost break-even, not sales-revenue profit break-even.

    Back to reference 4

  5. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Manufacturing Process Categories

    Addendum 5. A laser cut does not have to vaporize all the removed material

    Material may melt and be expelled from the cut; vaporization can also contribute. The classification depends on removal, not on which thermal mechanism dominates. TWI explains melt removal in laser cutting.

    Back to reference 5

  6. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Families

    Addendum 6. Why another book may show a different family list

    Other books may give composites a separate family, split glass from ceramics, or organize materials by bonding and structure. This collection keeps the instructor's four-family model. Engineered composites belong within Wood & Composites, including composites with no wood in them.

    Some materials fit more than one description. In the course's examples, plain concrete sits with Ceramics & Glass; steel-reinforced concrete illustrates Wood & Composites when the combined material system is the subject. Concrete itself also has a composite structure. State what is being classified rather than treating these labels as mutually exclusive scientific definitions.

    Back to reference 6

  7. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Families

    Addendum 7. A supplier value that checks the floating claim

    Plaskolite's OPTIX acrylic data lists a relative density of 1.19, with water as the comparison. This supports the conclusion that a solid piece is denser than water. Family descriptions are screening guides; use the actual grade's data for a design.

    Back to reference 7

  8. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Families

    Addendum 8. Hard to machine does not mean impossible to machine

    Corning's MACOR glass-ceramic is specifically designed for machining with conventional metalworking tools. That is a useful counterexample to a blanket claim that ceramics cannot be worked after forming.

    Back to reference 8

  9. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Properties

    Addendum 9. Stress, strain and modulus give the comparison units

    For a simple axial test, engineering stress is force divided by original cross-sectional area. Engineering strain is change in length divided by original length. Stress has units such as MPa; strain is a ratio with no unit.

    In a linear elastic region, the slope of stress against strain is Young's modulus, a measure of material stiffness. Yield strength concerns permanent deformation; ultimate tensile strength is the highest engineering tensile stress reached in the test. A nonlinear curve does not, by itself, prove that a material has no yield behavior.

    See Measurement Language for writing quantities and units consistently.

    Back to reference 9

  10. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Properties

    Addendum 10. Why a single “toughness number” needs its test method

    The area under a tensile stress–strain curve through fracture measures energy absorbed per original volume in that test. Impact tests and fracture-toughness tests describe related but different behavior. Temperature, loading rate and flaws can change the result, so compare like tests.

    Back to reference 10

  11. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Properties

    Addendum 11. Not every material has one useful melting-point number

    Pure crystalline substances can have a sharp melting point; many alloys melt over a range. Glass and amorphous thermoplastics soften over a range rather than showing a sharp crystalline melting transition. Thermosets and wood decompose rather than melting into a reusable processing liquid. Use material-specific processing and service data.

    Back to reference 11

  12. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Utilization and Cost

    Addendum 12. Why 20% loss means a 25% increase per useful amount

    If 80% of purchased material reaches the product, one useful unit needs 1/0.80 = 1.25 purchased units, not 1.20. State whether a waste percentage is based on purchased material or on the useful amount.

    Back to reference 12

  13. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Outsourcing

    Addendum 13. Why the cost boundary matters

    Reassigning unchanged overhead does not create a saving. Additional fixed spending can be relevant, and a benefit sacrificed by using a resource is an opportunity cost. See ACCA: Relevant costs and OpenStax: Relevant information for decision-making.

    Back to reference 13

  14. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Powder Bed Fusion in Polymers and Metals

    Addendum 14. Readable process sources

    The NIST PBF program documents metal laser powder bed fusion work. The polymer examples below use the public Formlabs SLS process description and HP's mechanism comparison. Vendor sources establish their stated systems, not universal rankings or machine settings.

    Back to reference 14

  15. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Powder Bed Fusion in Polymers and Metals

    Addendum 15. Why the support statement is qualified

    Ohio State's laser-PBF research summary explains support structures used to anchor overhangs and address thermally induced distortion in that context. A current Colibrium EB-PBF example documents process strategies that reduce or eliminate traditional supports for some applications. The exception is why this page states a case rather than an absolute.

    Back to reference 15

  16. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/What Is Manufacturing?

    Addendum 16. Why the boundary needs context

    Different industries draw the primary/secondary boundary differently. Here, use the raw-resource-to-stock and stock-to-part distinction. Extraction supplies the raw resource; mining alone does not turn ore into an ingot. A supplier's finished product can also be the next manufacturer's starting material.

    Back to reference 16

  17. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Choosing a Plastic Forming Process

    Addendum 17. Find the quantity where the two estimates are equal

    Set total costs equal: 900 + 14N = 18000 + 2N. Then 12N = 17100, so N = 1,425 parts. Below that quantity A costs less; above it B costs less under these assumptions.

    This model leaves out financing, mold replacement, setup changes, inspection, shipping and rejects. A flexible mold that must be replaced during a run adds another tooling cost. Recalculate when the assumptions change.

    Back to reference 17

  18. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Choosing a Plastic Forming Process

    Addendum 18. Further process-selection reading

    Formlabs' manufacturing-process overview compares form, volume and setup cost. Treat published volume ranges as examples, not universal cutoffs. The linked process references in Plastic Forming Processes explain individual capabilities.

    Back to reference 18

  19. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Conditioning and Finishing Plastics

    Addendum 19. Stress relief and crystallinity are different changes

    Residual stress is locked-in stress remaining after manufacturing. Heating can allow molecular motion that relaxes it. Some polymers, including PLA, can also develop more ordered regions during suitable heat treatment. Acrylic stress relief and PLA crystallization therefore do not share a universal temperature recipe. ACRYLITE's annealing guidance describes stress relief for its sheet. Prusa's annealing experiments show why dimensional change must be checked on printed specimens.

    Back to reference 19

  20. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Conditioning and Finishing Plastics

    Addendum 20. Other ways processors change plastic properties

    Industrial radiation treatment can crosslink selected polymers, but the result depends on the polymer and dose; some systems also undergo chain breakdown. Additives and reinforcements usually enter during material formulation rather than as a finishing step on a completed part. Fibers can increase stiffness, meaning a higher elastic modulus in the relevant direction, not a lower one. These changes require grade-specific data.

    Back to reference 20

  21. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Conditioning and Finishing Plastics

    Addendum 21. Why a clear surface can crack later

    Surface treatment can leave stress or expose existing stress to a solvent. Fine cracks may appear during later cleaning or bonding. ACRYLITE's edge-finishing guidance discusses polishing and compatibility; Prusa's ABS guidance identifies acetone smoothing for ABS. Choose a verified material/process pair, then check both appearance and fit.

    Back to reference 21

  22. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Conditioning and Finishing Plastics

    Addendum 22. Powder coating needs a complete substrate and cure system

    Interpon's heat-sensitive-substrate overview distinguishes powder-coating systems for heat-sensitive substrates, including thermal and UV curing approaches. A conventional metal-part powder cure is not a default recipe for a plastic part.

    Back to reference 22

  23. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Cutting and Machining Plastics

    Addendum 23. Why a slower cut can produce more heat

    A tooth that advances too little spends more time sliding against the work. The next tooth may also recut trapped chips. Useful chips carry some heat away, so reducing chip thickness without reducing rubbing is not a reliable cooling strategy. ACRYLITE's drilling guidance identifies low feed or excessive RPM as causes of melted chips; its routing guidance treats feed, cutting edges and RPM together.

    Back to reference 23

  24. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Cutting and Machining Plastics

    Addendum 24. Manufacturer references and the limits of a material list

    Trotec's unsuitable-material guidance lists PVC and explains why composition matters. Boss Laser describes acrylic's cut behavior, PVC decomposition concerns and polycarbonate edge discoloration. Universal Laser Systems' polycarbonate processing guide discusses reducing char through a specialized cutting method. A material name on a capability list does not establish a suitable setup for a particular sheet.

    Back to reference 24

  25. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/FDM 3D Printing

    Addendum 25. Where additive manufacturing fits the five course categories

    This course uses purpose to choose a primary category. Additive shape-building is Forming because creating the shape is the intended result; bonding between deposited roads is a secondary fabricating effect rather than joining previously separate parts. Other technical taxonomies organize these processes differently. The standard AM family name here is material extrusion. Subsequent support removal is Separating; annealing is Conditioning; sanding or painting is Finishing.

    Back to reference 25

  26. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/FDM 3D Printing

    Addendum 26. Material guidance is grade-specific

    Filament names describe families, not identical recipes. Pigments, fillers and blends change behavior. Prusa's material guide separates common filament families and their printing requirements. It does not establish what any particular shop printer can process.

    Back to reference 26

  27. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Joining Plastics

    Addendum 27. Why a clean-looking bond can peel off

    The bond is only as good as the material it touches. Mold-release residue, oil or an unsuitable coating can become the weak layer. Peel loads concentrate force at an edge; an overlapping joint can distribute load more effectively, although its dimensions still need validation. 3M explains low surface energy, and its bonding guidance shows why PE and PP are difficult, rather than impossible, to bond.

    Back to reference 27

  28. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Joining Plastics

    Addendum 28. Why heat alone does not guarantee a strong or sealed weld

    Temperature, force, time and joint fit work together. Too little heating leaves an unfused interface; excessive heating can degrade the polymer. Ultrasonic joints often use a small molded ridge, an energy director, to concentrate heating. A continuous-looking bead does not prove a leak-tight seam. Leister's extrusion-welding guidance identifies matching filler and joint geometry; Dukane's Guide to Ultrasonic Plastics Assembly explains energy directors for ultrasonic welding.

    Back to reference 28

  29. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Joining Plastics

    Addendum 29. Insert dimensions come from the chosen insert system

    SPIROL's hole-design guidance explains how oversized holes reduce performance and undersized holes can introduce stress or cracks. Its insert design guide distinguishes heat-installed thermoplastic inserts from other installation methods.

    Back to reference 29

  30. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastic Forming Processes

    Addendum 30. See the machine and cycle in a public explainer

    The BPF injection-molding explainer describes the machine and process. No shop-specific settings or procedures are implied here.

    Back to reference 30

  31. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastic Forming Processes

    Addendum 31. Three design clues to recognize

    • A shallow depression opposite a heavy rib suggests sink.
    • Scraping during release suggests inadequate draft or another ejection problem.
    • A sudden thick-to-thin step suggests uneven cooling and difficult filling.

    Protolabs' defect guide illustrates these relationships. Wall and draft requirements depend on resin, texture, depth and tooling; no single angle or thickness fits every part.

    Back to reference 31

    Addendum 32. Public process reference

    BPF: extrusion blow molding shows how the tube becomes a container.

    Back to reference 32

    Addendum 33. Public process reference

    BPF: rotational molding explains the sequence and the predominance of polyethylene.

    Addendum 34. Public process reference

    BPF: vacuum forming describes heating, forming, release and trimming.

  35. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastic Forming Processes

    Addendum 35. Public process reference

    BPF: extrusion profiles and sheet explains the die and downstream sizing equipment.

    Back to reference 35

  36. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastic Forming Processes

    Addendum 36. Public process reference

    The thermoset section of BPF's plastics-process reference explains the reaction under heat and pressure.

  37. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastic Forming Processes

    Addendum 37. Public process reference

    The polymer-casting section of Formlabs' manufacturing guide explains flexible molds and short-run economics.

  38. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastic Forming Processes

    Addendum 38. Public process reference

    ACMA's composite guide, Appendix E.1.1, explains wet hand layup and its dependence on workmanship.

    Back to reference 38

  39. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastics as Materials

    Addendum 39. Softening, melting and heat resistance are different questions

    Some thermoplastics soften over a range rather than having one sharp melting temperature. A part can lose stiffness and fail under load well before it flows. Thermosets also have service-temperature limits: being unable to remelt does not make them heatproof. Use the grade's data sheet for the actual load and temperature.

    The British Plastics Federation's thermoplastics reference explains reheating behavior and shows how varied the materials are.

    Back to reference 39

  40. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastics as Materials

    Addendum 40. Why a short strength test does not settle a long service life

    Temperature, time, moisture and chemicals can change both dimensions and load-carrying ability. A part that survives a brief pull may still creep over months. Curbell's dimensional-stability guide connects these effects to material selection.

    Back to reference 40

  41. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastics as Materials

    Addendum 41. Material references for checking a particular choice

    Compare BPF's thermoplastic families with supplier guidance for acrylic, polycarbonate and PETG sheet. Their grade differences matter more than a single generic strength number.

    Back to reference 41

  42. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastics as Materials

    Addendum 42. Where the resin comparison comes from

    The American Composites Manufacturers Association guide, Appendix D, compares composite resin systems. The resin holds and transfers load between the reinforcing fibers; the fibers and their orientation strongly affect the resulting composite.

    Back to reference 42

  43. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics/Plastics as Materials

    Addendum 43. Verified code sources and the standard's exact distinction

    ASTM D7611/D7611M-26, section 4.2, states: Resin Identification Codes are not “recycle codes.” Read the current ASTM significance-and-use statement.

    The number-to-material matches are published in the City of Sioux Falls RIC guide. The PET Resin Association consumer guide supplies the familiar label terminology. Checked October 27, 2026. This is an identification reference, not a specification for manufacturing compliant labels.

    Back to reference 43

  44. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Composites/Fiber Direction and Elastic Stiffness

    Addendum 44. How the axial stiffness is calculated

    Let m = cos θ and n = sin θ. For this plane-stress orthotropic layer, the compliance in the load direction is S̄11 = m⁴/E1 + n⁴/E2 + m²n²(1/G12 − 2ν12/E1). Then Ex = 1/S̄11 and εx = σx/Ex. The full stress and strain transformation supplies transverse and shear strain.

    Back to reference 44

  45. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Composites/Fiber Direction and Elastic Stiffness

    Addendum 45. Primary mechanics source and model boundary

    NASA Reference Publication 1351, Basic Mechanics of Laminated Composite Plates, sections I and II, defines isotropic and orthotropic behavior, develops plane-stress compliance and off-axis transformation, and identifies extension–shear coupling. Its stated scope separates elastic response from strength. The constants and examples on this page are original illustrative teaching inputs, not values from that report.

    Back to reference 45

  46. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Composites/Fiber Direction and Elastic Stiffness

    Addendum 46. How the laminate stiffness and the free-panel response are calculated

    Each ply's reduced stiffness Q (MPa) comes from E1, E2, G12 and ν12, and is rotated to the ply angle to give Q̄, using engineering shear strain γxy. With z measured up from the midplane and each ply running from zbottom to ztop (mm):

    A = Σ Q̄ (ztop − zbottom) in N/mm; B = Σ Q̄ (ztop² − zbottom²)/2 in N; D = Σ Q̄ (ztop³ − zbottom³)/3 in N·mm.

    The force resultants N (N/mm) and moment resultants M (N·mm per mm) relate to midplane strain ε⁰ and curvature κ (1/mm) by N = A ε⁰ + B κ and M = B ε⁰ + D κ. The interactive applies N with M = 0 and solves all six equations together. The drawn surface is w = −(κxx² + κyy² + κxyxy)/2, exaggerated by the stated factor.

    For the rose, a pull Nθ along direction θ has components (cos²θ, sin²θ, sinθ cosθ) Nθ. Flat-held: Ex(θ) = 1/(h · vᵀA⁻¹v) with v = (cos²θ, sin²θ, sinθ cosθ) and laminate thickness h. Free: the same, with the in-plane block of the inverted six-by-six A-B-D matrix in place of A⁻¹.

    Reversing the ply order (the bottom ply listed first) leaves A and D unchanged and reverses the sign of every B term, so the same pull makes the opposite curl. A single ply is symmetric about its own midplane, so it reproduces the one-ply result above: 40 GPa along the fibers and 10 GPa across.

    Back to reference 46

  47. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Composites/Fiber Direction and Elastic Stiffness

    Addendum 47. Primary mechanics source and model boundary

    NASA Reference Publication 1351, Basic Mechanics of Laminated Composite Plates (A. T. Nettles, 1994) defines balanced and symmetric laminates, derives the A, B and D matrices and the laminate constitutive equations, shows that a symmetric laminate has B = 0, and works an unsymmetric laminate example in which a tensile load alone bends the plate. It also notes that unsymmetric laminates can warp from processing temperature changes, which this lesson excludes. The ply constants, ply thickness, loads and panel size here are original illustrative teaching inputs, not values from that report and not design data.

    Back to reference 47

  48. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Bending and Laminating Wood

    Addendum 48. Why heat and moisture work together

    Moisture lowers the temperature at which the wood's matrix softens. This is why moist heat can make wood bendable without melting it. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory's Wood Handbook chapter on specialty treatments discusses plasticizing wood. Its Bending Solid Wood to Form compares species and bending conditions.

    Back to reference 48

  49. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Buying Lumber and Board Feet

    Addendum 49. Why the mixed-unit formula divides by 12

    Convert the length in feet to inches by multiplying by 12. Dividing the resulting cubic inches by 144 gives 12/144 = 1/12. The formula counts 144-cubic-inch units; it is not a linear-foot conversion.

    Back to reference 49

  50. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Buying Lumber and Board Feet

    Addendum 50. Reference resources

    • NIST: American Softwood Lumber Standard PS 20-25
    • Penn State Extension: Valuing Standing Timber, board-foot section
    • American Hardwood Export Council: hardwood measurement

    Back to reference 50

  51. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Choosing a Woodworking Machine

    Addendum 51. Why “router bit” is more useful than “end mill” here

    CNC routing can use end-mill-like spiral cutters, but routing also includes bearing-guided and shaped profile bits. “End mill” alone does not describe the tooling a beginning woodworker will encounter. Whiteside's template-bit range illustrates tooling for following patterns; its catalog also includes straight bits, flush-trim spiral bits and roundover profiles.

    Back to reference 51

  52. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Drying and Conditioning Wood

    Addendum 52. Why the indoor moisture target depends on the building

    The handbook's interior recommendations were developed from well-ventilated buildings without unusual moisture sources or air conditioning. Air conditioning and other building conditions can change the appropriate target. These are installation guidelines, not a universal kiln-drying specification; see Recommended Moisture Content, page 13–3.

    Back to reference 52

  53. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Drying and Conditioning Wood

    Addendum 53. Why dividing by the initial mass answers a different question

    30 / 230 × 100 = 13.0% gives the water fraction of the initial sample, not wood moisture content on the oven-dry basis. Wood MC can exceed 100% when water mass exceeds dry wood mass. The calculation does not set a suitable target for furniture. An actual oven-dry determination requires an appropriate laboratory method and equipment; these exercises provide the dry mass.

    Back to reference 53

  54. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Engineered Wood Products

    Addendum 54. Reference resources

    • APA: oriented strand board
    • APA: glulam
    • USDA Forest Products Laboratory: Wood Handbook (2021), wood-based composites

    Back to reference 54

  55. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Gluing and Clamping Wood

    Addendum 55. What “stronger than the wood” actually demonstrates

    In a well-made joint tested under a particular load, failure may occur in the surrounding wood rather than at the bond line. That shows the bond outlasted that wood under those conditions. It does not show that every adhesive joint exceeds every strength of wood, or that an end-grain butt joint is as strong as an uncut member. Grain direction, stress type, moisture, temperature and time under load can change the result.

    Back to reference 55

  56. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Gluing and Clamping Wood

    Addendum 56. Where to find product-specific instructions

    Consult the current label and technical data sheet. Titebond's application FAQs and the WEST SYSTEM filler-selection guide are starting points for their own products, not interchangeable specifications for other brands. For chemical handling, use Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets and Personal Protective Equipment.

    Back to reference 56

  57. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Grain and Moisture Movement

    Addendum 57. Reference resources

    • USDA Forest Products Laboratory: Wood Handbook (2021), moisture and physical properties
    • USDA Forest Products Laboratory: Wood Handbook (2021), chapter 13, Drying and Control of Moisture Content and Dimensional Changes
    • Oregon State Extension: Wood and Moisture Relationships

    Back to reference 57

  58. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/How Saws Cut Wood

    Addendum 58. Why tooth geometry changes the surface

    Across the grain, fibers can break beyond the intended cut if they are pushed away before being severed. Beveled teeth help slice those fibers. Along the grain, chip removal is a major concern. A blade's tooth shape, spacing, sharpness and feed all affect the result; tooth count alone does not identify its job.

    Back to reference 58

  59. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/How Saws Cut Wood

    Addendum 59. Blade terminology reference

    Ridge Carbide Tool's saw-blade design glossary defines gullet, kerf and hook angle; its top-grind guide compares tooth shapes. Choose a blade specified for the machine and cutting application.

    Back to reference 59

  60. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Milling Rough Lumber Square

    Addendum 60. Why a planer alone can preserve a bow

    Feed rollers can press a bowed board flatter during the cut. When the pressure is released, the board can spring back. Uniform thickness and flatness are different requirements. Specialized fixtures can provide a reference for other methods, but the sequence here assumes an ordinary jointer and thickness planer.

    Back to reference 60

  61. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Preparing and Finishing Wood

    Addendum 61. Further product-specific preparation guidance

    General Finishes' wood preparation guide is a starting point for that manufacturer's systems. Use the exact product's current instructions to choose the final grit and recoat schedule.

    Back to reference 61

  62. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Wood Structure and Species

    Addendum 62. What makes the cell walls work together?

    Cellulose reinforces the cell wall, while lignin and hemicelluloses help form its surrounding structure. This is a useful natural-composite analogy, but a tree is more complex than fibers suspended in glue. Cell arrangement, moisture, knots, and grain direction all affect a real board.

    Back to reference 62

  63. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Wood Structure and Species

    Addendum 63. How the cell structure differs

    Most commercial hardwoods have vessels, visible as pores in end grain, along with supporting fibers. Softwoods rely mainly on long cells called tracheids for support and water transport. These differences influence appearance and processing, but do not make every member of either group behave alike.

    Back to reference 63

  64. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Wood/Wood Structure and Species

    Addendum 64. Reference resources

    • USDA Forest Products Laboratory: Wood Handbook (2021), wood structure and species
    • American Hardwood Information Center: species guide

    Back to reference 64

  65. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Fasteners and Galvanic Corrosion

    Addendum 65. Sources for thread names and size examples

    McMaster-Carr explains inch diameter/TPI and metric diameter/pitch, including M6 × 1. Its UNC catalog identifies 1/4-20 as UNC. NASA's Fastener Design Manual (PDF), printed pages 12–13 / PDF pages 16–17, explains Unified coarse/fine series and thread classes. The manual is background on thread terminology, not a current procurement specification.

    Back to reference 65

  66. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Fasteners and Galvanic Corrosion

    Addendum 66. Why the wetted areas matter

    A small active area coupled to a large noble area can suffer concentrated attack when both areas contact the electrolyte. That is why coating only the active member is not automatically a cure: a small defect in that coating can leave a small wetted anode coupled to a large cathode. The relevant areas are those participating in the wet corrosion cell, which can change as a joint dries. A compatibility decision must consider the complete joint and environment.

    Back to reference 66

  67. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Fasteners and Galvanic Corrosion

    Addendum 67. Sources for galvanic contact, coatings and area effects

    ASSDA Technical FAQ 1 (PDF), pages 1–2, explains electrical contact, conductive liquid, coating defects and relative wetted areas. Hilti's Corrosion Handbook (PDF), printed pages 12 and 26–27, illustrates the cell, separation measures and environment-specific material pairing.

    Back to reference 67

  68. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Forming Metal

    Addendum 68. Sources for the casting routes

    The Steel Founders' Society of America glossary defines sand-mold features. The Investment Casting Institute's process overview (PDF) follows wax pattern, ceramic shell, pattern removal and casting. NADCA's die-casting FAQ explains pressure injection into reusable steel dies and suitable alloys.

    Back to reference 68

  69. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Forming Metal

    Addendum 69. Why a larger pattern does not replace a riser

    Pattern allowance addresses final size. Feeding addresses a different problem: a solidifying region may need more liquid metal to avoid an internal shrinkage void. A riser must remain able to feed that region. The diagram identifies parts of a mold, not a production gating design.

    Back to reference 69

  70. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Forming Metal

    Addendum 70. Cold forming does not guarantee an unchanged dimension

    Cold forming generally requires greater force than comparable hot forming. It avoids a separate hot-working step, but that does not prove every production cycle is faster. Springback, residual stress and later processing can change dimensions. Forging can also be hot, warm or cold; heat is not part of its definition.

    Back to reference 70

  71. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Forming Metal

    Addendum 71. Sources for solid-metal deformation

    The Forging Industry Association's Forging 101 (PDF) compares open- and closed-die processes and hot, warm and cold forging. Queen City Forging explains recrystallization and temperature classification. A Dartmouth-hosted metal-forming case study compares rolling, forging and drawing regimes. The Australian Aluminium Council's Extrusion Manual (PDF), page 10, explains flow through a die into a uniform section. Contenti's wire-drawing explanation (PDF) identifies pulling through progressively smaller openings; its operating steps are outside this selection overview.

    Back to reference 71

  72. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Forming Metal

    Addendum 72. Sources for sheet forming and flat patterns

    SSAB explains incremental roll forming and bending. 4Ming's forming handbook explains why low blank-holder pressure can allow wrinkling while excessive pressure can cause cracking. Mate defines blanking by the retained piece. SOLIDWORKS explains bend allowance, bend deduction and bend tables.

    Back to reference 72

  73. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Forming Metal

    Addendum 73. Porosity can be useful or unwanted

    Oil impregnation fills connected pores in a bearing so it can retain lubricant. Porite describes this use of porous sintered metal. That does not mean every powder-metal part is porous by design or that every part needs impregnation.

    Back to reference 73

  74. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Heat Treating Metals

    Addendum 74. Steel microstructures are not the four steel families

    Ferrite and austenite are different iron-based crystal phases. Cementite is iron carbide, Fe₃C, a hard, brittle phase. Pearlite is a layered arrangement of ferrite and cementite. Martensite can form from austenite during sufficiently rapid cooling in suitable steel. These terms describe structure, not the buying categories carbon, alloy, stainless and tool steel.

    Carbon can diffuse during slower transformations. Quenching can suppress those transformations and produce martensite. The outcome is not determined by cooling speed alone: chemistry and section size affect what forms throughout the part.

    Back to reference 74

  75. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Heat Treating Metals

    Addendum 75. Further reading on conditioning processes

    Bodycote's heat-treatment overview provides entry points for annealing, hardening, tempering, stress relief and solution-and-age treatments. AEC's alloy and temper guide is a starting point for aluminum terminology. Neither an overview nor a qualitative sketch replaces a material-specific process specification.

    Back to reference 75

  76. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Joining Metal

    Addendum 76. Sources for fusion welding, solid-state welding and the heat-affected zone

    TWI describes arc fusion welding and solid-state welding without melting the base metal. Its heat-affected-zone explanation identifies thermal changes in unmelted base metal.

    Back to reference 76

  77. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Joining Metal

    Addendum 77. Why MIG is a familiar name but GMAW is the broader term

    MIG refers to metal inert gas welding. GMAW also covers processes using active shielding gases or mixtures, often called MAG. Gas and filler selection depend on the alloy and process; the familiar shop name is not a complete welding specification.

    Back to reference 77

  78. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Joining Metal

    Addendum 78. Sources for the five process mechanisms

    TWI compares SMAW and GTAW arc processes and explains MIG/MAG wire feed and shielding, oxy-fuel fusion welding, and resistance spot welding. These are process explanations, not approved settings or operating procedures for a particular job.

    Back to reference 78

  79. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Joining Metal

    Addendum 79. Sources for the filler-temperature distinction and capillary joint

    The AWS Brazing and Soldering Manufacturers Committee defines the liquidus distinction and explains wetting and applications. TWI's vacuum-brazing overview describes filler flow by capillary action while the parent materials stay below their solidus, the temperature at which melting begins.

    Back to reference 79

  80. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Metal Stock Forms and Purchasing

    Addendum 80. Why an attractive surface can still be the wrong purchase

    A shiny bar can have the wrong alloy, condition, straightness or size allowance. Conversely, inexpensive hot-rolled stock can be a sound choice when later machining removes the scale and establishes the final dimensions. Compare total processing cost, not appearance alone.

    Back to reference 80

  81. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Metals and Their Properties

    Addendum 81. Why two pieces of the same alloy can behave differently

    Permanent deformation involves movement of crystal defects called dislocations. Grain boundaries, dissolved alloying atoms and small particles can obstruct that movement. Cold working and heat treatment change these obstacles. Composition alone therefore cannot tell you the strength of a finished piece.

    Back to reference 81

  82. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Metals and Their Properties

    Addendum 82. Why connecting two different metals can change corrosion

    When dissimilar metals are electrically connected in a conducting liquid, such as salty water, galvanic corrosion can accelerate attack on the more active metal. Material pairing, exposed areas and the environment matter. Isolation and drainage can be as important as the alloy choice.

    Back to reference 82

  83. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Nonferrous Metals

    Addendum 83. Source for the series table

    The Aluminum Association's aluminum-alloy overview identifies these series and their principal additions. It describes 1xxx as “aluminum 99 percent or higher purity.” The series names do not list every element in an individual alloy; for example, the Association also identifies magnesium and possible copper and chromium additions in 7xxx alloys.

    Back to reference 83

  84. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Nonferrous Metals

    Addendum 84. Sources and comparison limits

    The Aluminum Association identifies 6061 use in truck and marine frames and 7075 use in aircraft. Metal Supermarkets' 6061/7075 comparison supports the T6 tensile-strength comparison, tank and tooling uses, machinability and welding differences. Its fabrication discussion notes that restoring the weld area's original temper in 6061 may require further heat treatment and aging. Compare the supplier's data for the actual temper and product form.

    Back to reference 84

  85. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Metals/Types of Steel

    Addendum 85. Sources and quoted designation meanings

    The Metals Service Center Institute identifies the first digit as “family of steel,” the second as “additional elements,” and the third and fourth as “nominal carbon content”; its example is 1018 at 0.18% carbon. Total Materia's SAE-AISI introduction gives the final two digits as “the carbon content in hundredths of a percent” and lists 41XX as “Chromium-molybdenum steels.”

    The International Molybdenum Association's 304/316 comparison states that “Type 316 contains a molybdenum addition” and explains the corrosion benefit. Hudson Tool Steel's A2 data sheet describes O1 as “oil-hardening,” A2 as “air-hardening,” and D2 as “high-carbon, high-chromium.” These are introductory meanings, not complete material specifications.

    Back to reference 85

  86. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Manufacturing Documentation/Bills of Materials

    Addendum 86. Consumption, purchase cost and batch yield answer different questions

    You may need to buy a whole sheet even when one part uses a small fraction. That purchase is a cash requirement; the allocated fraction is the material estimate for the part. For a batch that consumes the entire stock unit, dividing its cost by the number of acceptable parts includes the loss from rejected pieces. Avoid charging the same waste once in the allocated share and again as an added allowance.

    Back to reference 86

  87. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Manufacturing Documentation/Critical Dimensions for the Shop

    Addendum 87. How to check a center when a caliper touches the hole edge

    Measure from the reference edge to the nearest hole edge, then add half the measured hole diameter to obtain that center coordinate. Use the same reference and direction as the drawing. This example does not specify a precision pin fit; a more demanding interface needs a more capable measurement method and a reviewed tolerancing scheme.

    The nominal hole spacing is 70 mm, derived from 85 − 15. The separate ±0.5 mm x-coordinate limits can allow spacing from 69 to 71 mm. If an interface needs a tighter spacing, the designer must change the requirements; the inspector must not invent a tighter limit.

    Back to reference 87

  88. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Manufacturing Documentation/Making Silicone Molds from a Printed Pattern

    Addendum 88. Where to find product-specific instructions

    Start with the manufacturer's product documentation, such as Smooth-On's technical bulletin and SDS directory. Its printed-pattern compatibility FAQ is a further-reading lead when investigating an uncured surface against a resin print. Check the complete instructions for the particular materials before selecting a treatment.

    Back to reference 88

  89. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Manufacturing Documentation/Operation Method Sheets

    Addendum 89. Why there is no universal operation order

    A feature may become inaccessible after assembly; a coating may need to be applied first. A larger blank may help holding, but its final cut must preserve the reference used for the holes. Record the reason for a departure from the usual sequence. The five process categories describe kinds of change, not a fixed order.
